TALE OF THE TOES. , Baby is clad in his nightgown white, Pussy-cat purrs a soft good-night, t- And somebody tells, for somebody knows The terrible tale of ten little toes. BIGHT FOOT. This big toe took a small boy:, Sam, \ Into the cupboard after the jam • This little toe said, "Oh, no, no \ " This little toe was an-xious to go; This little toe said, " "Tisn't quite right;" This'little tiny toe curled out of sight. LEFT FOOT. . This big toe got suddenly stubbed; This little toe got ruefully rubbed; This little frightened toe cried out "Bears I" This little timid toe, "Run upstairs !" Down came a jar with a loud slam! slam! This little tiny toe got all the jam. lb—Leeds Weekly Mercuru. CLARA. G. DouvArr.

BUTTERCUPS. Have the sunbeams all unknowing, Taken root on earth, and growing, '77: Flowered in yellow buttercups, for the children's praises? Do the moonbeams, resting lightly On the quiet meadows, nightly Blossom into daisies? Bonny buttercups, beguiling, z. Human sorrow with the smiling -- - Of their round and winsome faces in the —saddest daytime ; Offering to each new-comer Golden salvers full of summer, All the sunny May-time! How they nod and smile and glisten, As they turn their heads to listen: To the whispers of the breezes lingering above them; t: A Giving their long-hoarded treasure • In such free, unstinted measure, Who could choose but love them? ......_ To no chance of birth beholden They will blossom, fresh and golden, By the wayside--cheery welcomes for the:traveller keeping; And uplift their sunny faces 7 On the quiet resting-places Where the dead are sleeping. Oh! to'live through life's brief day-time, Like the buttercups in May-time, Loving earth, yet growing sunward still through joy and sorrow, ° And like them, with trust unshaken, Fall asleep at night, to waken In a glad tomorrow! My Rowles, in the Girls' Own Paper.

eggs." - Little Charlie was having a wordy war with his nurse. His father sang out, "Now, Charlie, are you going to be quiet, or shall I come with a rod ?" "Never mind the rod, papa," responded the youngster, " I can set herright without whipping her." It takes eight hundred full-blown roses to make a single table spoonful of the famous perfume, and you can get enough perfume out of an onion to drive a dog on the gallop out of a slaughter-house. And yet we admire the rose more than we do the onion. A physician, passing a gravestone cutter's shop, called out—" Good morning, neighbour, hard at work, I see. You finish your gravestones as far In memory of,' and then wait, I suppose, to see who wants a monument next." "Why, yes," replied the old joker, "unless some- body's sick, and you are doctering 'ern, then I keep right on: A gentleman, recently calling at a boarding-house, left his umbrella in the hat rack with a card on which was the following :—" Belongs to a man who strikes a forty- -pound blow. Will be back in five minutes." When he returned the umbrella was gone, but in its place was a scrap of paper bearing the words—" Taken by a man Who walks five miles an hour. Won't be back at all." A young mother, in despair of ever teaching her idle little girl, aged four, her letters, and thinking that per- haps-the child knew more than she would admit, said— "Now, Katie, I won't try to teach you to-day. You shall be mother, and teach me my letters." "-May I really and truly be mother ? " said Katie. "Yes, my darling.' "Let us begin then," was the response. "You have been a very good child to-day, and you may have a whole holiday," and Katie shut up the book and ran off laugh-

Without it, learning is pedantry, and wit impertinence; and even seirtue itself looks like weak- ness wanting discretion. The best parts only quality a man to be more sprightly in errors, and active to his own prejudice.—Addison. A LITTLE GIRL'S HEART. How should the heart of a little girl be? As pure as' the lily that blooms on the lea, As clear as the dews from the heavens that fall, As true as the mirror that hangs on the wall, As fresh as the fountain, as ga-y as the lark That trills cut it's song 'twixt the day and the dark, As glad as the angels, when soaring they fly -On the bright wings of love to their home in the sky. —From the German. Lord Beaconsfield, in one of his novels, tells us the . House of Lords resembles a house of butlers. This was emphatically true as regards the personal appearance of Lorditedesdale. the far and justly famed Chairman of Committees of the Upper House, whose death was re- cently -recorded. On one occasion his lordship went to pay 'his wine merchant's bill; on leaving: he was pre- sented with a• ten-pound note. "What is this for?" asked'his lordship. "Oh. it is what we always allow the butler," was the reply. The story goes that his lordship toolethe money, and ever afterwards paid his wine bill bimeelf. There is a curious anecdote, says Temple Bar, told of Baron Martin, who, when travelling on the Western Cir- leuit, dined with a church dignitary, at Winchester. The evening passed pleasantly, but, after bidding his guest sood-riight, the warden said to a friend—" The judge is a man of great common sense and shrewdness; but for a gentleman he is the most ignorant man I ever met. Me hadeaever heard of William of Wykeham." As Baron Martin drove away in his carriage he said to his marshal —" We'll, for a learned man, the warden is the most ignorant man I ever met, for he did not know that John Day had-stables at Daneburv." ,-...F.-e.•.;44e,61;..Pth HE'D CHOOSE TO BE A BART.—The followinc, story was told at the recent•encampment of the Grand Army at Mexico, Missouri. A group around one of the numerous camp-fires were relating incidents of bravery and -cowardice-shown in battle, and this is one df them:—"lt -was at the battle ,of Gettysburg," said the speaker, "when the bullets were falling like hail, and the shells were shrieking and bursting over our heads in a way to raake the bravest heart tremble, a private dropped out of the ranks and-Skulked back toward the rear. He was 'well under way, when, unfortunately for him, he was met by General Slocum coming to the front. 'What are you doing here? Get back to your post,' the General .shouted. The poor-fellow stopped still and trembled like a leaf, but made no reply. 'Get back to your post, you miserable coward; aren't you ashamed of yourself to be skulking back here when you should be in front with -your brave comrades?' Still the -man made no reply, but commenced to cry like a year-old infant. 'You in- famous, sneaking coward,' shouted the infuriated Gene- ral; 'get back to your post. I'll ride you down like a dog. Why, you are nothing but a baby.' 'I-I-I'll t-t-tell • you what, G-g-general,' said the blubbering fellow, 'l'd $-g-give anything just nea-now if I was a b-b-baby, and i-i-if I had my ch-ch-choice, I'd r-r-rather be a female b-b-b-haby." Toseneu FOR A ‘WIFE.—Dr. Dunlop and his brother the captain, old bachelors, lived together on their estate -at Galbraith, near G-oderick, Canada West, with a re- ," 4aaectable Scotch body, as the doctor called her, for their , —*housekeeper. Now, whether any. scandal had been 'raised, or whether the doctor thought it would conduce 1, -to their .greater comfort if he or his brother were to .1 -marry the housekeeper, or whether he meant, only for a e. joke, to tea.ce his brother, does not appear. Be that as it may, thedoctor proposed—in consequence, as he said, of some unpleasant remarks and their lonely situation— for some one of them to marry her. "Now, Sandy, you know i would almost as soon hang myself as put my head into the anatrimonial -noose, yet I think it only fair -to stand my chance. So what I propose is, that each of us shall toss up a copper three times, and he who has the most heads shall be free." As this appeared a very fair propositien, the .captain at once consented to the ar- rangement, and they immediately proceeded to bring this friendly contest for a wife to an issue. The doctor 'would not have caasented to run the risk of losing his !iberty if he had not been perfectly sure of winning; for Somel2l.7_a chance he had become the possessor of a copper 711 n head on either side; so, when they came to toss uP. as might be expected, the poor unconscious captain , was -duly elected for matrimonial honours, to the great ' glee of the - roguish doctor • who, no doubt, chuckled aver his successful stratagem. Strange as it may ap- pear. the captain honourably fulfilled this singular en- gagement. The large consignment of polled cattle for the Messrs. Geary Brothers, which left this country at the end of last month, has reached New York safely. At Renfrew cattle fair last week trade was stiff and prices low. Ayrshire cows sold from £l2 to £l7, or 20 per cent. below the prices of some years ago. Mr. Stephenson, Balliol College Farm, Newcastle, has purchased a pair of promising yearling polled heifers from Mr. 8.. J. Mann, Skelton, Boroughbridge, Yorkshire. Some important sales of Herefords were held at River- view Park, Kansas, last month. The first day 12 bulls sold for an average of £55 each, and 35 cows and heifers for nearly £65 each. SALE OF SHORTHORNS AT BURGHLEY PARIL—The bulk of the herd of shorthorns belonging to the Marquis of Exeter has been offered for sale at the Dairy Farm, Burghley Park, the auctioneer being Mr. John Thornton. Twenty-five cows and heifers were sold, and eight bulls. I Unfortunately no high prices were realised; the top I figures among the cows were reached by Sea Gull 2nd, 36gs. ; Lady Blanche sth, 34g5.; and Sea Mew, 32gs. Of the bulls, Yosemite 3rd and Tollendale 4th, bred by the Duke of Manchester, reached 32gs. and 30gs. respectively. Dtrrcri CATTLE.—The deep-milking properties of Dutch cattle, a breed widely distributed throughout Holland, greater part of Belgium, a portion of North Germany, Denmark, and the United States, are well known. Dutch cattle are of an exceedingly useful kind, and at the head of all breeds for abundant milk-yield. This gives them a peculiar value to butterine manufactures, and in cer- tain branches of the legitimate dairy business. Where milk is sold by the (ninon, or a medium quality of cheese is produced, Dutch cows are perhaps more profitable than any other sort. But where butter and a rich, fine 'quality of cheese are desired, some other kinds answer th • dairyman farmer's purpose far better. Taken all round, the Dutch cattle are fairly good. The cows retain their copious milking properties for a longer period be- tween their calvings than any other breeds we know of, and in addition, their calves make a heavy carcase of „good veal, whilst the cows fatten into fair weights of a useful sort of beef. In the large dairy districts of America, pure Dutch cows and crosses therefrom are in great favour. For many years past importations of the very best Dutch cattle into the United States have been on an extensive scale, and it is there that some of the finest specimens of the breed are now to be found. When a large fine herd of these cattle are seen together they certainly present a most picturesque appearance, and form a very pleasing subject for both pen and pencil. Not long ago a Scotch Board School Inspector asked the members of a class that was under examination, "What is the cause of the saltness of the ocean ?" Flushed with the discovery that had flashed upon her mind, one little girl raised her hand. "You may tell," said the inspector. "Salt fish, sir !" exclaimed the pupil, triumphantly. Monsieur X. has a little falsetto voice. The other day in giving a coin to a blind beggar on the corner, he said in his flute-like voice—" Here, take this, my poor man." "Thanks, madame." answered the blind man. "I am not a lady," replied M. X., in a vexed tone, with his voice pitched in a still higher key. "Thanks, mademoiselle," returned the mendicant. The laws of social welfare press on all of us, whatever may be our condition. Something speaks to us, above all voices of human authority, in condemnation of sel- fishness, in defence of liberty and truth, in favour of justice and generosity. Only as we obey this still small voice, only as we listen attentively to catch its more distant tones, only as we exercise our faculties to dis- cover its full meaning, are we able to interpret it for others, or to urge them to obedience. (2) Never follow anyone blindly; make sure what it is you are asked to do, and what purpose is to be served by doing it. (3) Always think of what the thing you are tempted to do would lead you to, and where it would land you at last. (4) Follow the leadership of no one who sneers at those whom you know to be good people. div.head: ANCIENTS AND IaHE DOMESTIC
div.p: THE ANCIENTS AND IaHE DOMESTIC
FOWL. There are only two references in the Old Testament to the domestic fowl, and from the fact that it does not

__- occur in the writings of the ancient writers wadi about 400 or 500 years before the Christian era it is probable that it was about that period ere it found its way west- ward from Persia, whence it had been taken from India. _ _

Darwin states that it is figured on some of the Baby- lonian cylinders, for Mr. Layard had sent him an impres- sion of those dating from the sixth or seventh centuries, and also on the 115,rpy tomb in Lycia about 600 n.c., from which fact he thinks that the fowl reached Europe some- where about the sixth century. The first actual refer- ences in western literature to the fowl occurs in the
writings of Theognis and Aristophanes between 400 and 500 B.C. But fowls had evidently gone eastward at an earlier date. It is mentioned in an ancient Chinese _ _

encyclopedia which is said to have been compiled 1,400 years before Christ. This earlier migration is to ba easily understood from the geographical positions of China and India, much more favourably situated for intercommunication than India and the western nations.

It is also surprising that there is no reference on the Egyptian monuments to the fowl, and this fact may be taken as proof that it was not then in that coun- try, for these monuments are otherwise so full of the details of ancient housekeeping on the Nile. There are to be seen flocks of tame geese being driven home from the pasture. They and their eggs are being carefully counted, but nowhere cocks and hens; and when Aristotle and Diodorus say that eggs were artifi- cially hatched in Egypt by burying them in dung, they must mean the eggs of geese and ducks, or refer to a later period than the Persian conquest, which Diodorus seems to hint, for he commences his account of the hatching ovens with these words—" The Egyptians in- herited many customs relating to the breeding and rear- ing of animals from their forefathers, but other things they have invented, among which the most wonderful is the artificial hatching of eggs. It is probable that by the time of the Christian era, that is, during the interregnum between the closing of the canon of the old Testament , and the opening of that of the New Testament, the fowl had spread itself all over the western parts of Asia and the eastern parts of Europe at any rate, though it was known in western Europe. The reference to the crow- ing of the cock at the time of Peter's denial of our Lord could only have reference to the domestic fowl, and this reference is made in such a manner as to show that there was nothing remarkable in the crowing of the cock, but that it was a sound heard daily. We can as- sume, therefore, that the migration of the fowl into Syria and eastern Europe took place within the six cen- turies prior to the advent of Christ, and that by the commencement of the Christian era it had become fami- liar and one of the ordinary domestic animals." The original home of the fowl was India, and it first migrated west with the medo-Persian invaders. In a work on the temple of the Samian Hera, Menodotus says that as the cock spread from Persia, so the sacred pea- cock spread from the temple of Hera to the surrounding districts. In the religion of Zeroaster the dog and the cock were sacred animals; the first as the faithful guardian of herds and flocks, the second as the herald of dawn and the symbol of light and the sun. In Hehn's work on the wanderings of plants and animals we learn that the cock is specially dedicated to Craosha the heavenly watchman, who awakened by fire, awakens the cock in his turn; he by his crowing drives away the Daevas, evil spirits of darkness, particularly the yellow, long-fingered Bushyacta, the demon of sleep. A passage in the bundehesh runs: " Halka the cock is the enemy of the devs and magicians. He assists the dog, as it is written in the law. Among the earthly creatures that plague Daruj, the cock and the dog unite their strenktli. He shall keep watch over the world, even as if there were no dog to protect the flocks and houses. When the clog and the cock fight with Daruj, they weaken him, who, else, would torment men and animals. Therefore, it is said, by him the cock shall lall the enemies of goodness be overcome; his voice scatters the evil." Wherever a Persian settled he took 1 as much care to procure a cock as to pray and wash be- fore and dyring sunrise. As far as the limits of the Persian dominion reached, there, no doubt, the tame and useful, easily transported, and at the same time so pecu- liar creature, found a welcome in the households of non- believers. On the so-called harpies monument from the Acropolis of anthurin Lycia (now in London) there is the figure of a god to whom a cock is brought as a gift or sacrifice. If this monument, as archreologists sup- pose, really belongs to a period before the taking of Xan- -1 thus by the Persians, then the Lycians must indeed have I been acquainted with the cock before the spread of the iPersian dominion. If the domestic fowl had been fami- liar to the Lycians long before the Persian time, the Greeks must have shared in the knowledge; but neither in the works of Homer and Hesiod, nor in the fragments of the elder poets, is there any trace of cock or hen. Surely among people who had no clocks, the prophet that proclaimed the hours by night, the proudly strut- ting, winking, crowing Sir Chanticleer, the supremely jealous sultan surrounded by his harem, the hot vain- glorious champion armed with his comb, tassels, and spurs Dame Partlet announcing to the world her last achieve- ment; all this merry parody of a human family and aristocratic manners could not fail to be a frequent sub- ject of description and comparison, had the poets any opportunity of observing it. It did not escape even the ancients, that Homer, though he used the proper names Alector and Alectroyan, seemed to know nothing of the fowl so-called. It has been already stated that the first actual refer- ences in literature to the fowl are in the writings of Theognis and Aristophanes. As regards the former of these two writers, he throws doubt on the references, in that there is so much that is spurious in his poems. He , regards the portions as having been added at a later date. But in the writings of Epicharmus, who lived during the period of the Persian wars, and in those of Simondes, Aschylus, and Pindar, we find the cock, already men- tioned under the proud name of Alector, as the usual companion of man. The fights between cocks became a striking example for poets as soon as the fowl was a familiar object. In the "Eumenides" of /Eschylus, Athena warns the Athenians against civil war as re- sembling the combats of cocks. Pinder compares the i inglorious victories of civil war to the victories of a barn-door fowL And it is stated that Themistoeles aised the courage of his army by reminding them how two fighting cocks risk their lives, not for the hearth and its penates, but for fame alone. When afterwards the public cock-fights, which are represented on innumer- able ancient monukents, were supposed to be derived from the above speech of Themistocles, it proves at least that cock-fighting was not thought of as older than the , Persian wars. The comic poets still call the cock the , Persian bird. The cock first appeared at a late ' period when mythic production was just dying out, in consequence of which it could never attain any prominent religious importance. As a fighting I cock it was sacred to Ares and to Pallas Athena. Plutarch states that at Sparta, on the close of a cam- paign, two kinds of sacrifice were in use; he who had attained his end by craft and persuasion sacrificed a bul- lock; he who had gained it by fighting, a cock. At Olympia the figure of a cock from the hand of Onatus, announcing or signifying the sun, was to be seen on the shield of Idomeneus, who was the.grandson of Pasiphie, and therefore a descendant of the sun-god. Plutarch speaks of an image of Apollo, with a cock perched on one hand, the symbol of the god of the sun. On the coins of the Phiestus in Crete may be seen the figure of a youth- ful god, evidently a personification of the sun, holding with his right hand a cock which sits in his lap. Plato's thr IzeA sdkoi ehpa si 0 st tuhgeh gt oedv eor yf ho ne ael itnhga.t t lAI es ucpo ecrks twi tai os nsacri fipeculiarced to the rocky town of Methana, between Epidauros and Troezen, mentioned by Pausanias, is likewise connected with the worship of Apollo in that district. To avert the evil influence of lips, the south-east wind, on the vines, two men would cut a cock in halves, and each run with one half in opposite directions round the vineyard, and then bury the bird on the spot where they met. Soon after the appearance of cocks and hens in Greece, whole families of fowls must have been transported to Sicily and South Italy, and there, as in Greece, spread from house to house. The oldest representations of the cock on coins and vases in Greece, Sicily, and Italy never go beyond the second half of the sixth century B.c.

Why are pawnbrokers like pioneers of progress? Be.. • cause they are always ready to make an advance. There is one thing about a house which seldom falls, but never hurts the occupant when it does. That is the rent. In the private journal of a lady recently deceased were found these words :—" I expect to pass through this world but once. Any good thing, therefore, that I can do or any kindness I can show, to any fellow-creature, lee-me do it now. Let me ,not defer or neglect it, for I These words are worthy where Way we can see them every day. Each shall not npoltacpa placed ds this ay again. day, each week, each year comes but once. The foresight which regulates expenditure to suit the income and apportions it carefully to the needs of a family, forgetting none of the many claims, is a valu- able power, and one which every wife and mother especially should cultivate. The very same income, managed with intelligent method, or spent with impul- sive carelessness, ratty make all the difference between a happy home, where peace, comfort, and prosperity reign, and a scene of contention, self-reproach, misery, and ruin. In the long run it will be found that it is early, thorough, and persistent discipline that tells. Now and then genius, aided by extraordinarily favourable condi- tions, blazes forth into some kind of temporary success and notoriety. But the possessors of such fame are almost certain to settle back eventually to their merited plate of mediocrity. No man can .truly be said to be great when his fame rests upon an accident or upon a single achievement. It is the slowly but well-built tower of work and character, reared piece y whole lifetime,•that forms the enduring monument of b piece during a i real greatness. NEWTON RACES.

When the Stewards of the Jockey Club, with a laudable desire to check the "undue multiplication of meetings," limited the Newton fixture to two days instead of three, they undoubtedly improved the meet-• lug in a racing.point of view. Whilst they patted it on the back with one hand, they slapped it on the face with the other ; for a Newton Meeting on any other days which do not include Friday can never be popular in the district in which it is held, and the reason is, the employers of labour refuse to close their places of business at the beginning of the week whereas they are ready and willing to do so at the week end. The holiday character of .the Newton Meeting is, therefore, for the present destroyed ; and, as a matter of course, a considerable portion of the revenue derivable from the holiday people is destroyed alwo, for the simple reason that they cannot be pre- sent. This has especially been the case on the pre- sent occasion. The announcement that the races were to be on Tuesday and Wednesday created a re- vulsion of feeling against the week being considered as a general holiday in Earlestown and district, and a canvass of the men employed at the Viaduct wagon works—the principal workshop—resulted in favour of work being continued on the race days. This deci- sion caused an alteration in othei respects, for the ma- jority of the Sunday school officials shortly afterwards decided to have their annual treats, &c., at Whit week, instead of in race week as formerly. This at once took away the general holiday character of race week. But notwithstanding this fact a large number of the local workmen "asked off" for the afternoon of each day, but more particularly was this the case on Wednesday—the " Cup day." On each of the two days several penny shows, shooting galleries, and other " attractions" were erected on Earlestown Market Place, and drew the attention of a considerable number of people. There was a very large ieflux of visitors from Liverpool, Manchester, Warrington, Wigan, St. Helens, &c., while special excursions arrived from Preston, Birmingham, Leeds, and other places. The arrangements at the railway station were of a most complete and satisfactory char- acter, and there was little delay in the ordinary train service. The local officials were reinforced by a large staff of inspectors and porters from other stations. The special trains, after their arrival at Earlestown, were principally shunted into the sidings, near the Viaduct Works, until they star- ted on their return journeys. The streets of Earles- town about noon and in the evening of each day pre- sented a very animated and busy appearance. There were the usual compliments of busses, wagizonette-s, and vehicles of every kind running to and from the races, while the almost nece6sary adjuncts to all race meetings, in the persons of three-card "sharpers," gamblers, thieves, pick-pockets, and vagabonds, of every diseription were present in large force. On Tuesday the weather was Yery unfavourable, and rain fell during the whole of the afternoon, but there was a marked improvement on the following day, when rain fortunately held off. TUESDAY.

The annual races at Newton Common commenced on Tuesday, when there were a sufficient number of horses to ensare some good sport. The meteorological outlook, how- ever, was the reverse of encouraging, as rain fell heavily during the night, and continued more or less throughout the afternoon, which made the paddock a perfect quagmire, while the going was very holding. Under such circum- stances it was not surprising to find the attendance below the average, the falling off being chiefly noticeable in the ranks of the public. THE GREEK QUESTION.—RAISING THE BLOCKA.L+E. ATHENS, SATITEDLY.—Tne Government has resolved to reduce the army to a peace footing, bat, it is argued, to comply with the desire of the Powers would be to establish a Principal of foreign interference in the internal affairs of this country which the Government cannot countenance. It is further pointei out that the resolution to disarm was aadopted after mature deliberation, and surprise was there- Ise expressed that the Powers should make difficulties about raising the blockade, especially as Turkey is com- Pistely satisfied, and has notified the same to the Powers. .the relations between Greece and the Porte are cordial, and M. Tricoopis has received a reply from M. Condouriotis Stating that the Sultan has ordered the prisoners to be im- tnediately surrendered to the Greek authorities. Orders have likewise been sent to Ahmed Eyoub Pasha to evacuate Positions. On the other hand, the Greek troops con- tinue their retreat from the frontier. The number of men killed in the Larissa division in the recent fighting was 26. At the fighting at Tricala 16 were killed. CONsuarrmoPLz, SAT ORDAT.—The Turkish troops are new being withdrawn from the Greek frontier. The in- tention of the Porte is to proceed to disarmament as soon as the Greek demobilisation is complete. CONSTANTINOPLE, MONDAY.— The Porte to-day des - Patched a fresh Circular ta the Powers cmaplaining of the dilatory manner in which the Greek disarmament is being oarr;ed out. Suspicions are entertained in diplomatic circles here that Greece is anxious to retain Zigos, which corn- bands the town of Mltzovo, and that this accounts for the tontinuance of the blockade. VIENNA, MONDAY.—M. Tricoupis wishes to retain thirty thousand men under arms, which the Powers consider far too high a number if the Greek force is to be reduced to a genuine peace footing, and the danger of a renewed out- break is to be effectually removed. The Exchanae Telegraph Company learns that a telegram received in London from Paris announces on the most trustworthy authority that the Powers, acting chiefly at the instance of the French Government, have resolved to raise the blockade of the Greek coast within a few dove. THE FIGHTING ON THE GREEK FRONTIER. LIST OF CASUALTIES. CONSTANTINOPLE, TUESDAY.—A.ccordinz to the official "Porto! Ahmed Eyonb Paeha, the Turkish commander, Abe casualties on the Turkish side in the recent engage- tnents on the frontier amounted to 7 officers and 160 men killed and 13 officers and 162 men wounded. The report add that the number of Greeks buried in Ottoman territory 18 1,161, while Greek prisoners include one major, two cap- tains, six lieutenauts, and 310 men. AU the prisoners have been despatched to the barracks at Salenica by order of the aultan, and receive the same rations as the Turkish soldiers. The majority of the prisoners were taken at

Diezeros. 8-15 P.M.—M. Condouriottis, the Greek Minister. to-day assured the Porte ••b It the continued occupation of Zigos by the Greeks was the result of a misunderstanding. and that orders had now been given for the evaCuation of the posi- tion. Some of the Ambassadors have made similar commu- nications to the Porte. THE SOUDAN. WADY HALFA, MONDAY.—NO further news has been re- Calved from Dongola concerning the reported intention of the dervishes to advance with a considerable following upon this place. Sheikh Saleh, of the Kabbabish tribe, reports that on account of the barren and uncultivated state of the province of Dengola the immediate advance of a large force is impossible. THE CHOLERA IN ITALY. ROME, SATIIRDAY.—The cholera returns show 33 cases and 31 deaths at Venice yesterday. THE ERUPTION OF MOUNT ETNA. Roma, SecrunDay.—The eruption of Moant Etna seems to be subsiding. The stream of lava has stopped in its pro- gress not far from Nicolost, ail& hope is reviving that the town and adiacent country may be saved. SPANISH NAVAL ARMAMENTS. MADRID, SIINDAT.—The Minister Of Marine has drawn up a complete scheme of naval atmaments for Spain,' to axe- cute which he proposes to demand an extraordinary credit Of £9,000,000, to be spread over a period of nine years. The Minister calculates that at the expiration of the first four years Spain would possess a navy comprising one iron- clad, 25 cruisers of various kinds, 100 first-class and 50 Efecend-class torpedo vessels, besides 93 other vessels and gunboats. THE CANADIAN FISHERIES DISPUTE. WASHINGTON, MONDAY.—The Government has decided not to enforce a penalty upon the fishing schooner Sisters, of Yarmouth, Nova Sootia, which was recently seized at Portland, Maine, for violating the Customs regulations. The vessel has left for Yarmouth. Nsw YORK, MONDAY.—A. telegram horn Portland pub- lished here announces that the Nov* Scotian schooner Sis- ters sailed thence to-day with her flag flying. The expen- ses which the captain had to pay were trivial. Nsw YORE, TuzsmaT.---Her Majesty's ship Bellerophon has arrived at Halifax, it is supposed, for the purpose of protecting the Canadian fisheries. A Spanish fishirg-beat, the Clotilde, has been seized off the coast of Florida for vio- ktinn of the shore Ibnit, ad is now detained at Caber Key,.

Florida, pending the receipt of instructions from Washing- ton. The New York Tribune publiehee a report that the ' North Atlantic fleet will shortly be ordered to the Canadian • coast. The journal adds that several Gleuceeter schooners are believed to be in danger of capture for the violation of the Dominion Fishery Laws. FRANCE. THE EXPULSION OF THE PRINCES. PARIS, MONDAY.—The Committee charged to examine the Princes Expulsion Bill to-day elected M. Madier de Montjau as its president. The discussion on the expul- sion question will probably be taken in the Chamber on Saturday. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—To-day the Committee on the Ex- pulsion Bill after a long' discussion agreed .upon the three ' main principles which it will recommend the Chamber to ' adopt. It first decided by six votes to five that the Expul- sion Bill should be compulsory and not permissive; secondly, by the same number of votes, that it should apply to all members of farmer reigning families, and not merely to individual persons; and thirdly, also by six votes against five votes, that the decree of banishment should be pro- nounced by the Legislature and not by the Executive. PARIS, THURSDAT.—The committee upon the bill con- cerning the expulsion of the Princes not having yet drafted its proposals, the Ministers were not able to deliberate upon the subject at this morning's Cabinet Council. It is be- lieved that the Cabinet will maintaie the proposal for the immediate expulsion of the direct Legitimist or Bonapartist pretenders, with power to expel the other Princes ehottld such a measure be deemed expedient. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR.—REVOLUTION AT TANANARIVO. PARIS, THTTRSDAY.-1 he " Intransigeant " says the Gov- ernment has received alarming intelligence from Madagas- car. On the proclarnatian of the treaty with France a revolution \ took place at Tananarivo, and the Prime Minis- ter, who was friendly to France was overthrown. ALIENS IN THE UNITED STATES. WASHINGTON, WaneasnaT.—The Senate has unnni- mousier passed the bill for preventing aliens from acquiring lands in any territories belonging to the United States Gov- ernment. THE SOCIALIST RIOTS IN AMERICA. Cnece.ao, WEIDNDeDAY.—SeveraI more Anarchists have been indicted here and at Milwaukee in connection with the recent riots. Eight arrests were made at Milwaukee to- day, including three members of the Executive Board of the Knights of Labour. THE PACIFICATION OF BURIVIAII. RANGOON, WEDNESDAY.—The "Rangoon Gazette" pub- lishes advices from Bhamo stating that Colonel Fitzgerald's expedition against the Kachyans, near Bhamo, had reached Paung Twang, ten miles from Katran, the Sawbwa's capital, and in the fighting they had killed 20 of the rebels besides wounding a number of others. Oa our side one man only was wounded. The Sawbwa had tendered his submission and made propitiatory offerings, apologising at the same time for his people's conduct, and vouching for their future good behaviour. He remained three days with the column, , which, having effected its purpose, returned to Bhamo. MARRIAGE OF PRESIDENT CLEVELAND. WASHINGTON, WEDNESDAY MIDNIGHT.—The guests at President Cleveland's wedding this evening consisted prin- cipally of the near relatives and the Cabinet Ministers and their wives. Mr. Garland, the Attornev-General, although invited, was not present at the ceremony. The bride, Miss Agnes Folsom, arrived at the Executive mansion about half- past sii. At a few minutes past seven President Cleveland, with his affianced on his arm, came unattended down the western staircase, and, passing through the corridor, entered the apartment known as the blue room, which was elabo- rately decorated for the occasion with flowers from all parts of the world. The bride wore a dress of ivory satin, trimmed, the corsage with India muslin. The marriage ceremony was proceeded with without delay, Dr. Sutherland, the min- ister of the Presbyterian Church, which President Cleveland attended, officiating, being assisted by the Rev. Mr. Cleveland, the President's brother. The service began with a prayer, invoking the blessings of the Almighty God on the pair. This was followed by a brief address on the solemnity of the marriage relations ; then, after the usual formal in- quiries, the couple were declared man and wife and the ser- vice was then concluded with the benediction pronounced, by the Rev. Mr. Cleveland, a presidential salute of 21 guns being fired immediately afterwards. The usual congratula- tions followed, during which the celebrated marine band played the 'Metal Chorus and the march from Lohengrin. The President and his wife then led the way into the spa- cious east room, whence the company proceeded to the family dining-room of the mansion, where a sumptuous wedding supper was served. The wedding presents were numerous, but in deference to President Cleveland's wisites, were not exhibited. The President's gift to his bride was a diamond necklace. After bidding their Mende a hasty , goodbye, the bride and bridegroom drove off amid a shower of rics to the railway station on their way to Deer Park, Maryland, where they will spend the honeymoon. They will be absent about a week. There are general rejoicings throughout the country, and congratulations have been received from all parts. The President received a telegram from Queen Victoria, at Balmoral, conveying her Majesty's hearty felicitations on the hapay event.

Having quoted from one of Mr. Chamberlain's speeches, the hon. member asked the right hon. gentleman to explain how it WAS that altlknugh in February he was prepared to undertake "an immense operation " for the pacification of Ireland he now objected to the partial operation proposed by the Prime Minister. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN moved the adjournment. THE MEDICAL ACTS AMENDMENT SILL.—VICTORIA UNI- TERSITY.—The House having resumed Committee on the Medical Acts Amendment Bill, Clauses 1 to 6 inclusive were agreed to.—On the motion of Sir L. PLAYFAIR, the word "six," giving the number of Crown nominees on the General Council, was omitted, and the right hon. gentle- man moved to substitute " five."—The amendment fixing the number at five was then agreed to.—Sir H. ROSCOB moved an amendment for giving Victoria University a repre- sentative on the Council instead of the collective represen- tation with Durham University provided by the bill. He said those Universities were totally different in character, and Victoria University was a young, new, and flourishing Institution , with which was connected two successful, well equipped, and numerousty attended medical schools, where the scientific education was of the highest class. Besides Owens College there was the Liverpool University College, and it was hoped the Leeds Medical School, connected with the Yorkshire College, would shortly join them. Durham was entirely remote from their centre, and the education it gave was altogether inferior.—After some discussion the Committee divided. For the amendment, 11.9 ; against, 42.—After some further discussion progress was reported. The West Indian Encumbered Estates Bill and the British North American Bill passed through Committee and were road a third time. The Jurors Detention Bill passed through Committee. The House adjourned at 2.50. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tusspay. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack a a quarter-past four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—EAri CADoG&Ir moved that the exam- iner's certificate of non-complitince with staging orders in the case of the Gravesend and Northfleet Docks and Rail- way Bill should be referred back to the Standing Orders Committee The proposed works, be said, would give em- ployment to a large amount of idle labour.—The Duke of Buckingham (chairman of committees) was in favour of maintaining the standing orders.—The Marquis of SALIS- BURY supported the motion, remarking that the standing orders "were not brought down by Moses from the moun- tain," and were not so sacred that they could not be put aside ; but the Earl of KIMBERLEY said the authority of the Chairman must be supported.—The motion was rejected by 54 to 52.—Earl SPENCER moved the second reading of the Arms (Ireland) Bill, and in reply to obseryations mode by various peers on the Trish policy of the Government, said he did not think there was at the present moment suffi- cient active crime in Ireland to justify fresh repressive measures.—The motion was agreed to, and the bill was afterwards read a third time and passed.—The Crofters (Scotland) (No. 2) Bill was read a third time and passed. The House adjourned at ton minutes to nine o'clock, until Friday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. EXPENSES OF PARLIAMENTARY ELECTIONS.—Mr. LABOU- CHERE asked the Prime Minister whether, in vieel of the fact that appeals were being made to the rich for funds to conduct the next general election, he would, in order to enable candidates to stand whose private means were small, introduce a bill to secure to the constituencies full freedom in the selection of candidates by throwing the necessary ex- penses of elections upon the entire cemmunity.—Mr. GLAD- STONE replied that under existing circumstances he was not able to to enter into any engagement for the introduction of a bill, but he was friendly to the principle, and thought it very hard on the working classes that in a country which was so liberal as to make provision for a num- ber of political pensions for salaried public offi- cers, which pensions were often held by men of birth and station, when the labouring men desired to return a member of their own class they should have to pay the ex- penses of his election, and likewise support him presu- mably, while he is engaged in the discharge of his public duties.

THE HOME RULE BILL. Sir M. HICKS-BEACH inquired when the debate on the Government of Ireland Bill would be likely to terminata.— Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply, proposed that they should, by general consent, have an arrangement that it should ter- minate on Monday night. Mr. T. P. O'Coamon resumed the debate on the motion for the second reading of the Home yule Bill, and argued that whether the bill were passed or not there was no possi- bility of Ireland obtaining separation from England. He further contended that the idea that a Home Rule Parlia- ment would at once proceed to establish and endow the Roman Catholic Church was dead and buried, and past all resurrection. He deplored the action of the senior member for Birmingham, but his letter had not been published, and viewing its importance the House had a right to see the letter, The Prime Minister had promised to introduce I another bill in the autumn, in which he would not be free to abandon the principle of a legislative assembly sitting in Dublin nor the five essential conditions by which it was accompanied; but he was free to propose, or to accept if proposed by another, , any other plan for carrying into effect that principle and' those conditions. The vote would be taken on the naked principle of the bill, so far as it might be clothed with con- ditions necessary for the safety of the Empire and the pro- tection of minorities. Mr. O'Connor then read a letter from Bolton to show that daring the recent electien the- Tory party there gave pecuniary aasistance in the publica- tion of National League literature and election documents. A large number of Tory candidates asked for the Irish vote on the ground of no coercion for Ireland, and in January the same party came in with a policy of coercion. The hon. gentleman proceeded to give further carious particulars as to the relations between the Tories and the Nationalists . at the late election.—Mr. WINTERBOTHAM said he had come to the conclusion that there was nothing in the measure which ought to lead a Liberal or a Radical to support it. , He wanted to see it distinctly set forth in the bill that the Irish Parliament was to be subordinate to the Imperial , Parliament, so that there should be no mistake on that point.—Mr. BRADLAIIGH insisted that a vote against the second reading of the bill would be a vote against its prin- ciple and not dgainst any method.—Mr. Matcauratat re- marked that the bill went beyond his views, but after the recent statement of the Prime Minister he felt justi- fied in voting for the second reading. He should however, unless some better provision were made for the preservation of the integrity of the Empire and the supremacy of Parliament, vote against the bill at a later stage.—Mr. WODRHOUSE said he was dead against the prin- ciple of the bill. He thought it remarkable that no one had discovered what a tremendous failure the union of Eng- land and Ireland had been until December last, when Mr. Parnell was returned with 85 followers. The debate was continued by Colonel Nolan and Sir J. Goldsmid.—Mr. J. MORLEY asked the Liberal opponents of the bill if they thought that any modus vivo:di could be found between the Liberal party and hon. gentlemen opposite who were in favour of 26 years of coercion. Mr. ILLINGWORTH moved the adjournment of the debate, which was agreed to. The Lords' amendments to the Crofters (Scotland) N 0.2 . Bill and the Infants Bill were considered and agreed to. The House continued sitting until a late hour.

THE HOME RULE BILL. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN resumed the adjourned debate on the motion for the second reading Of the Government of Ireland Bill. After the meeting at the Foreign office some of them hoped that the bill was dead, and that it woald never be re- vived again in its present shape. They hoped that advan- tage would be taken of the interval to recast and remodel the measure. In that case they might have abstained from active opposition. But that hope had vanished. He gathered from the speeches of the Prime Minister that the bill was not to he remodelled, that it would not die, but was to re- main in a state of suspended animation; that it was to be introduce 4 again in October, and that there was to be no change in the scope and main lines of the bill. He held that if they supported the second reading they would be logically and honourably committed to support the same or a similar bill when it should be introduced in October, and they would be committed sot only to its principles but to the main outlines and general plan of the bill. He had been charged by the Attorney.Greneral with having been a few years ago in favour of the exclusion of the Irish members from Westminster. That was an entire mistake, and arose from a misreported answer he had made to a question dur- ing his canvass at Sheffield in 1874. The whole tenour of his speeches at that time was in favour of a federal basis on the lines of Mr. Butt's Home Rule plan. He thought it extraordinary that his late colleagues should bring such a charge against him after twelve years while there was hardly one of them who held the opinion which he entertained on this question twelve weeks ago. He had always laid stress upon the re- tention of the Irish members, because he had felt that the effect of the bill was that it not only created a Parliament in Dublin, but destroyed the Imperial Parliament in West- minster. If hon. members did not want the Imperial Par- liament to be supreme, they were right in voting for the bill. The Irish members wanted to weaken the supremacy of Parliament and to throw a doubt upon it. On the ques- tion of Ulster the Irish members had said they would rather have no bill at all than one which did not place Uls- ter under the power of the dominant majority at Dublin, and which did not give them in Dublin the power to tax Ulster. Was that fair to Ulster? If the resistance of Ulster was expressed in the usual constitutional way to any proposal for submitting them to a Dublin Parliament they ought not to ignore it. Loyalty must be at a discount when a pas- sionate allegiance to the unity of the kingdom was made a moral offence and a crime by a Minister of the Crown. He had been told by the Attorney-General that be was fan- ning the flame of religious bigotry. He had said that the people of Ulster had some fear for their religious and ma- terial interests, and he contended that be was right. He had always been joined with those who would destroy every shred of religious ascendancy, and he contended that the Catholic Church by its tenets and by its faith was bound not to be content with equality, but to demand predominance. Proceeding to deal with other proposals in the bill, the right hon. gentleman remarked theft there was no hope of the finality they had been promised in connection with this legislation. Much as be disliked the bill, lie thought if it contained what was likely to be accepted as a final settlement he would vote for the bill, but he did not believe there was any finality about it. "If the Irish members said they accepted it as a final settlement they could not bled the Irish people. Until they' came to separation they could not stop gee pacify the de- mands which were now put forward. He illtd been asked for an alternative scheme, and he would give them one. They might find the lines of it in the present constitution of Canada. The relations between the several provinces of Canada and the Dominion Parliament ware such as be was prepared to establish between England and Ireland. His objections to the bill as it stood were unchanged, and as he could not see that what had been suggested by the Prime Minister would meet those objections he felt it his duty to vote against the second reading The threat of a dissolu- tion bad no terrors for him. Of one thing he was confident, that the Union majority in the House wozald be strengthened. During the controversy two things had been made clear— one that the British democracy had a passionate devotion to the Prime Minister, and the other was the sentiment in favour of some form of Home Rule for Ireland which would give to the Irish people greater control over their own affairs. On these two principles the British democracy were practically unanimous, but they were not unanimous upon the method by which it bad been soueht to establish the principle. It was upon the method and the plan of the bill that they were going to the country, and not upon its principle. (Cheers.) Mr. SEXTON stigmatised Mr. Chamberlain as an ally of the Tories, a confederate of the Whigs, a deserter of his own party, one who contrived the downfall of the Prime Minister, the break-up of the Liberal party, and the destruc- tion of the efficiency of that party as an instrument of pro- gress. The debate was centinned by Mr. Craig-Sellar. Mr. bee, Mr. Dawson, Mr. Magniac, and other hon. mem- bers. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER deprecated the view taken by many of the opponents of the bill, that the proposed separate Parliament for Ireland meant a separa- tion of the two countries, and the disintegratioe of the United Kingdom. Those who took that view must have forgotten that Irelabd bad had a separate Parliament of Its own. He pointed out that the Ant for the establishment of the Dominion of Canada, of whose plan Mr. Chamberlain was in favour, gave much wider powers than were proposed by this bill. The policy of the Government was one of confi- dence in the Irish nation, that of Lord Salisbury was the policy of defiance and distrust. Mr. T. P. O'Cosmos moved the adjournment of the debate. The House adjourned at a quarter-past one. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The base was made at twenty-five minutes past twelve o'clock. ASCENSION DAY.—Mr. J. THE HOME RULE BILL. Before the renevialof the adjourned debate on the Govern- ment of Ireland Bill, Sir H. TYLER asked whether it would not be contrary to practice and order to waste time on fur- ther discussion of a bill which was admittedly dead; but the Sesexzet replied that nothing had come to his know-. ledge which should interfere with the regular procedure on the bill. Mr. IL H. FOWLER, who was received with cheers, re- sumed the debate. In reply to the attack on the tactics of the Government, he pointed to the precedent set by Mr. Disraeli on the Reform Bill in 1887, in accepting a second reading subject to fandamental alterations in Committee. Turning to the argdanents used by opponents of the bill, he denied that it would impair the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament, which he ineisted could not denude itself of one jot or tittle of its power, or pass any law which it could not subsequently repeal The House was asked to deal not with a legal but with a practical problem, and they had not got to confront abstract theories, but to deal with a living peo- ple. (Ministerial cheers.) Lord J. MANNERS drew attention to the inadequacy of the safeguards in the bill for the protection of the Protestant minority, and, objecting to the constitution of the proposed Irish Parliament, contended that at the end of 30 years the Irish peerage would cease to be represented in it. Mr: F. STEVENSON maintained that the bill would pro- mote the true unity of the empire, and Colonel HUGHES. ALLETS, who opposed the bill, dwelt upon the action of the National League, which, he argued, was mainly respon- sible for the present difficalty. Mr. STOREY complained of the reticence of the leaders of the Opposition, and twitted the Whigs with playing into the hands of the Tory party. He prophesied that the bill would be defeated, but insisted that in the end a similar bill would be passed by one party or the other. Mr. Mevereotrene objected, as an Irishman, to the bill on the ground that it would place Ireland in a degraded and humiliating position, and that it opened the door to absolute separation and independence. • Mr. GRAY protested against the assertion that the Na- tionalists desired to seized upon Ulster on account of her wealth, quoting statistics to show that according to all the tests that could be applied Ulster was by no means the best favoured part of Ireland, whilst emigration from it was greater than from any other Province. SHOCKING COLLIERY FATALITY.—ONE MAN KILLED AND ANOTHER INJURED.—Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest on Wednesday forenoon, at the Owl's Nest, Blackbrook, on the body of John Hedkinson Aged 15, coup- ler, and residing at Blackbrook, who was killed in the New Boston Colliery, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., on Saturday last. Mr. H. Hall (her Majesty's inspector of mines), Mr. B. Glover (colliery agent), and Mr. S.Woods (miners' agent) were present.—Deceased's father, who works In the same pit, said he was in the place where the accident happened only a week before, and it appeared "right enough."—Williana Byatt, aged 16, stated that John Camp- bell, of Earlestown, deceased, and himself were engaged filling up an old working, and had taken two boxes of rub- bish in. The second box was tipped up, when a large quan- tity of roof suddenly fell, and they were all three buried. Witherll was dug out first, then Campbell, and then Bodkin- son, but the latter was dead. There were props in the place, but no bars.—James Coombes, day wageman, said he was working 40 yards away. He heard a shout, and went to the place. He assisted to get out those who were buried. Wit- ness was working in the place, and at the very spot, on Fri- day afternoon, and considered the roof perfectly secure. There were two loose ends in a distance of 18 yards between, and the fall took one loose end. He considered there was plenty of timber set.—Sareuel Blinton, fireman, said he sounded the place at 9-45 on Friday night and 4-30 on Sat- urday morning. He then considered it safe, and could not account for the fall.—Richard Unsworth, another fireman, who examined it at six o'clock, was of a similar opinion.— Campbell, the other injured man, was unable to attend.— Mr. Hall said he bad examined the place, and considered the witnesses had given a fair description of the y circum- • ••••• jrit 41 stances.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Mao do"' Sr, Hum cus Wi RAILWAY SLSILL.. TUNE 5,1886 Helens and Wigan, Junction Railway Bill, with amerd- ments by the promoters, was considered and ordered for third reading. luis REGISTRATION.—Mr. Dmote moved the second reading of the Registration of Totem (Ireland) Bill. He said that the object of a Registration Bill should be to get every one entitled to vote on the list at the lealt possible expense, and so as to leave little opinion for the ingenuity of the lawyers and agents to defeat that purpose. This bill was drafted on the experience gained at the last registration with a view to achieve that object. That was a provision which, though it seemed revolutionary, was one that he had always insisted upon. The payment of rates and the securing of Parliamentary votes were two different things, and he had always believed that the joining of them together was a radical mistake from the outset.—Mr.:LEwts moved that it be read a second time this day six months —Colonel WARING seconded the rejection of the bill.—Sir C. Daze said he should like to see the bill applied to England as well as Ireland.—After discussion, Mr. J. MORLEY said there had been no opinion expressed contrary to the propriety of the bill to Great Britain. In its present position, the Government intended to bring in a Registration Bill which should deal with the whole of the United Kingdom, and he therefore reserved his opinion as to the expediency of passing a bill which re- lated to Ireland only.—After some remarks from Sir J. Councillor FRANCOMB said that on Sunday last-a circus came into the town and for some reason or other they were placed in a field at the back of the Conservative Club. He did not know who ordered it, but at 12 o'clock they all bad to shift again to an unsuitable piece of land covered with water. The men had been travelling all night yet they were compelled through some red tapeism to work all the Sunday afternoon. He also found the Corporation ser- vants with the water carts and it was really more like a fair day than anything else. The horses, he believed, could get no water to drink for some hours, and at 12 o'clock the Corporation water carts had to be got out to give the ani- mals water. Considering that the Markets Committee got some sort of toll from these travelling people he thought it was their business to make some provision for them. (Hear, hear.) If he had been at home on Sunday morning he should have given those animals all the water he ceuld get from all the taps in his house. Councillor ,UTTON corroborated the remarks of Councillor Francomb, and said that when he asked Mr. Place the rea- son for shifting the circus he said the piece of land had been mistaken. He said if he (Mr. Sutton) had been there he should have advised them not to move at all, as it created such confusion. With regard to water, they were actually kept waiting till half past twelve o'clock at noon. Mr. Place and Mr. Norman said they had been to Mr. Ross and he had refused to let them have any water although there was a hydrant there. (" Shame.") He told them distinctly they should not have any water and that they might get it where they could. Mr. Norman had therefore to get out the Corporation water carts to provide the animals with water to drink. Councillor HUTCHINSON said that Mr. Place, the market- inspector, wrote to these people to say what piece of land they had to go on and he (Mr. Hutchinson) did not think Mr. Place or the Markets Committee were to blame for the mistake that had been made, As tett the water, he thought the circus people, knowing the number of anitnals they had, I ought to have an agent in advance to see that provision is made for water. He did not think there was any blame to be attached to Mr. Place, the Markets Committee, or even to Mr. Ross (" Oh, oh," and "Oh yes, every blame.") Alderman BURGESS said that was the first word he had heard of the water carts being used for that purpose, but he ' was deligkted to find that etr. Norman could, on his own esnonsibility, do a thing of that kind. (Hear, hear.) It redounded very much to his credit. In-all probability he would bring the water from the hydrants set aside for public purposes, and that Corporation would be called upon to pay for the water, because it was measured to the pint almost. (Laughter.) Alderman Burgess also suggested that the Markets Committee skould see that there were sufficient means of ingress and egress in the tents erected by circus companies, Jac. Councillor BROADBENT said these circuses formed a delightful and ienocent source of amusement to the people of Warrington, and it was a great advantage they should come to Warrington. On that account, he hoped that in the future every reasonable care would be taken to afford then, that sort of convenience and accommodation they were en- titled to. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR said that in that case Mr. Place could hardly be blamed, as he wrote to the circus authorities pointing out to them as clearly as he could the precise locality of the ground they were entitled to go upon. The worst thing was the absence of water for these animals. Mr. Ross, ow- ing to same peculiar notion of his own—it might be con- scientious—resolutely declined to let these poor animals have water, and the officers of the Corporation were reduced to the necessity of conveying water in the water carts. He (the Mayor) thought it was a matter to be deplored and hardly creditable to Warrington that such a state of things should exist—(hear, bear)—and he hoped it would be a means of hurrying the Corporation on to endeavour to de- vise some means by which they could get hold of the water- works. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then confirmed. SHE GAS COMAIIVFEE.—REDUCED PRICE OF TAR. The Gas Committee reported as follows :—Resolution that the tender of Messrs. Joseph Turner and Company, Limited, of Queen's Ferry, for the purchase of tar for one year, at 8a 4d per ton, be accepted, subject to the conditions of a contract to be prepared by the Town Clerk and satis- factory guarantee of £5OO as security. The average illumi- nating power of the gas for the past four weeks was equal to 17 89 crannies at both works. Alderman Holmes, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, referred to the tender for tar which had been ac- cepted, and said this was a very low price indeed. The price they obtained last year was 21a 3d per ton, and the year before 30s. When they took into account that they produced something like a thousand tons of tar in the year they would see that it must make a serious diminution in their revenue. When tar was so cheap it was found chea- per to heat their retorts with it than to use coke so that they bad adopted that course with it at the Mersey-street works, but they were not able to do it at Longford. Alderman WBBSTER seconded the adoption of the min- utes.

Councillor W. PIERPOINT asked how much tar they made at Longford and bow much in Mersey-street. Alderman HOLMES : I should say we make rather more at Longford than at Mersey-street. Councillor W. PIERPOINT said that as there seemed to be a very serious depreciation in the price of tar he thought it would be better not to manufacture so much gas. He be- lieved they were manufacturing gas and selling it at about cost price to keep the Longford machinery going, and he would surest whether it would not be better to close Longford altogether. They would not then have that defi- ciency of £5OO a year on tar at Loneford. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Pierpoint also complained that two promises that had been made to him by the Chairman of the Gas Commit- tee had not been carried out. One was that cards should be supplied to each consumer of gas, upon which the figures should be entered on each visit of the gas inspector. 'I he next promise was that a report should be furnished to him with respect to two gas accounts. He had received a , memorandum signed by Alderman Holmes, but he could not look upon that as a report from the Gas Committee. He thought he had a right to expect a report and not a mere memorandum of a few lines. Alderman Homers, in reply, said that cards were now being issued, and with regard to the report, he was surprised that Mr. Pierpoint should feel so touchy about it. He thought Mr. Pierpoint would have been satisfied, and at any rate nothing in the shape of a slur was intended. The minutes were then confirmed. PROPOSED NEW RIVER WALL. The minutes of the Rivers Committee contained the fol- lowing :—The "London Gazette," April 16th, 1886.—Mer- sey Conservancy, 8, Rtchmond-terrace, Whitehall, 14th April. 1886.—The Commissioners for the Conservancy of the river Mersey hereby give notice, pursuant to the 9th section of the Act 5 and 6 Victoria, cap. 110, intituled " An Act for the better preserving the navigation of the river Mersey," that they have received from Mr. Wil- liam Owen, of Warringt n, architect, a notice, given pursuant to the provisions of the above- mentioned Act, of h:s intention to erect a river wall at Atherton's Quay, Warrington, Lancashire, on the fore- shore of the river Mersey, a copy of which notice is sub- joined.—T. SPRerr, Vice-Admiral and Acting Conservator. —"I, William Owen, of Cairo-street Chambers, Warring- ton, associate of the Royal Institute of British Archi- tects, practising as an architect, surveyor and valuer, do hereby give you notice that I intend, after and subsequent to the 15th day of June next, proceeding with the erection of a river wall at Atherton's Quay, Warring- ton, Lancashire, in accordance with plans deposited in the office of the Commissioners for the Conservancy of the River Mersey, Whitehall, London, for and on behalf of Messrs. Monks. Hall and Company, Limited, iron manu- facturers, Warrington, the owners of the land; such wall to cemmenee a little to the north-east of the sewer outlet be- longing to the Corporation of Warrington, at Bank Quay, Warrington, and to run in a south-westerly direction, for a distance of about 850 lineal feet, ard to commence again at the Corporation sewer outlet at Atherton's Quay, War- rington, and to extend in a south-westerly direction about 450 lineal feet. The walls to be built according to section and plan deposited with you, and to be composed of Run- corn or other approved red sandstone and slag from the iron works. WILLIAM Ow."—Minute, That after an inspec- tion of the plans and aections submitted by Mr. Wm. Owen, it was considered desirable that the works should be done, and it was resolved that so far as the Corporation was:con- cerned the plans and sections be approved. Alderman CROMELD, in moving the confirmation of these minutes, said, referring to the above-mentioned proposal, the tide bad completely washed the footpath away. In his time, he should think, five or six yards of the

WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB. ANNUAL DINNER. The annual dinner in conneciou with this club was held at the Conservative Club-room, Sankey-street, Warrington, on Tuesday evening, when about too persons sat down to a good repast, served up in capital style by Mr and Mrs Speakman. the manager and manageress of the club. The chair was occupied by the President of the club, Councillor R Fran- comb, and amongst those present at the dinner and the subeequent proceedings were Councillors W Pier- point, Wright, and Satton ; Messra H Ashton (eap- tain of the club), T Locker, T Pemberton. J E War- ren (hon. sec.). J R Wye& (ex-sec.), J Whittle (cap- tain of A team), T Barnes (umpire), F Webster, and J C B Savage (auditors). re Smith (treasurer), S Wright (umpire of A ream), J Liehrnan (club repor- ter), Fair. Turner, W Speakman, E Gilbert, T Davies, W Hayes, W Povey, W Dillon. Frank Turner, S Hough, E Dillon, J Massey, J Buxton, J Jolley, R Henry, W Ford, J Critchley, W Hughes, W Gray, .T Brimelow, J Burgess, A Jolley, W Pickles, Bashford, kc. Letters regretting inability to be present were read from Mr Parr (Grappeuhell Reyes), Mr T Mor- ris, Mr R Fairelough, and Mr G Riley. The CHAIRMIN, in proposing the health of the Queen, referred to the visit of Her Majesty to Liver- pool on the oceasion of the opening of the exhibition in that city, and to the bravery she evinced by ap- pearing in an open carriage during the heavy rain. He was sure it was a treat to see the people receive Her Majesty with Furth hearty cheers. Expressions were eon- gently heard from people that they hoped no ill would happen to the Queen during the inclement weather. The kindness of her M ijesty in becoming' patron to the ,Seamen's Orphanage fine other institu- tions in Liverpool chewed them that the Queen took an interest in every portion of her p.2ople. (Hear, hear) The toast was received with musical honours, and tbe toast of the Prince and Princess of Wales was then given from the chair, and received in a hearty manner. Mr. J. Carreneev proposed "success to the .e.lifrai- rington Football Club." It gave him, he said, great pleasure to submit the toast, especially after the suc- cess that the club bad achieved clarieg the past sea- -1 son. Of -all the years that he had been conneeted with the elub the last one was, he thought, the best, and, considering the good form and abilities the players had shown during the lest season, he thought they took rank as the premier club of West Lanca- shire. (Hear. hoer.) He hoped the the clue would continue to progress, that the members would keep united, and that they would win sdll greater fame. (Applanse.) Mr. BAIIRES, in responding to the toast, said that the club had had a chequered career, but had now won a prominent position. It had not, however, reached the first-class position that it was destined yet to reach, especially if the word " Union " was written as its watchword. At the present time the club was passing through a crisis. He hoped the crisis would not be of a dark character, but that the club would come out of the fire purer than had hitherto been the case, and that during the coming football season it would command the attention of all the people of Warrington. (Applause.) Mr. W. Dillon teen sang a song composed by Mr. Joseph Dillon, in which the merits and achievements of the club were extolled. It w is received with great favour, each verse being followed by a round of applause. din g t to o The CHAIRMAN then announced that medals were to be t distributedoce distributethe m emtm members °let et shaei d" that thept T the Team." ' medals' ha d p been won simply by perseverance and determination. If they wished to achieve a victory there was nothing like Putting on a bold front, and being determined to do it.. (Hear, hear.) He was afraid that they had got a little across since winning the cup and the medals, but they must not let trifling things break up such a good club— (hear, hear,)—as their first team, and such promising teams as the "A team," and others that were following up. (Ap- plause) He once heard a tale of someone saving to an old lady "How do you manage to bring on such a big femilv and keep them BO geletly and nicely together? " and she replied "Why. everyoue of us love the youngest the best, and by that means there is no one jealous." They must, if possible, all love the first team the best, and also nurse the young ones, who would soon take the place of the first . team. He believed that if they bad got up a match between , the first fifteen and the next twenty-five they would have ;;.-1 brought out one or two very conspicuous players. The • great thing in football was union—every man should play to win the game. and not for his own elorificstioe. (Ap- plause.) They should all play so that the club, arid not in- a dividuals, might shine. He deprecated praise being given lavishly to individual members of a team at the expense of others, and urged that the " 15 " shou'd play as one solid mass, for the more solid they were the more suc- cessful must they be. They were all exceedingly proud of the men who kicked goals and made special points, but those men must not think they alone had won the game or the cup. Every man had his place and his work, and every man should have the honour that was due to him. He did not wish to introduce anything that would in any way spoil the harmony of the evening, but they would ex- cuse him saying th At banded together they were strong, but divided they would go to th 3 wind. (applause.) He hoped that the club would he very successful in the future, and that any slight difference that might tend to mar the suc- cess of the club would be sunk. (Applause.) The medals, gold ones, of a pretty design, each having inscribed on tbe back the name of the player, were then distributed, the names of the recipients being :—Messrs. Ashton, W. Povey, T. Barnes, J. Buxton. J. Jolley. J. T. Massey, W. l illon, Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, T. Davies, E. Dillon, Speakman, E. Gilbert, W. Myer., and J. Rigby. 'Mr. H. Boardman, who took the place of Massey (injured at Southport) in the final,wat presented with a silver medal. Each members! the team was heartile ch,eered on receiving his medal. The medals have been supnlied by Vaughton and sons, of Birmisehem. After their distribution Mr. Cal- vert gave a short but interesting entertainment, and Mr. Savage sang "Ehren on the Rhine." Mr. ASHTON, in acknowledging the presentation of the medals, said that the club had had many conflicts, and had met Mermen worthy of their steel. The first engagement they took part in was an easy matter, and then they con- tested with a really first-class club, and, he need not say, ~ they won the match on the'r merits, and were the best team. , When the final was played he thought they met almost one of the best teams of the North of England. Their form with Aspull the afternoon that they won the cup was cer- tainly good, and he thought, candidly speaking, that War- rington was the best team. Mr. Ashton then referred to a statement made by the captain of the Runcora club to the effect that they had not fair play at Widnes, and also that they had not had fair treatment from the Union. He (Mr. Ashton) thouebt that if any one club bad not proper treat- ment it was the Warrington club. (Applause.) Be trusted that the Warrington club would again go in for the cup next year. If fortune smiled upon them they might again wile. the cup. (Applause.) Mr. S. WRIGHT proposed the health of the chairman, and referred to Mr. Francomb's services as president of the club. The Chairman hev'ng briefly replied, the room was pre- pared for dancing, which was afterwards indulged in with I spirit.

CONTLICT BBTIVBEN SOLDIBRS AND CIVILIANS IN DUB- LIN.—On Sunday night a seriotss disturbance took place in Publin, between a number of Scots Guards and civilians. The row began in a low quarter of the city, and it was continued into Sackville-street and other leading thorough- fares. The soldiers were reinforced by comrades, and the number of cicilians rapidly increased so that in a short time an extensive riot was going on: The mob used stones and sticks, while the Guardsmen resorted to their belts and fists.
