The MAYOR said that be had received a communication asking that Town Council if it would petition in favour of the second reading of he Manchester Ship Canal Bill in the House of Lords, but as the second reading had taken place the previous night there was no necessity for the petition now. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS: What was the date of the commu- nication ?
The MIYOIt It is dated 24h May. PROICOTIOX TO COXSTABLES.
The Watch Committee recommended that P.C. Robert Shaw be promoted to the rank of Bergeant, and P.C. Mona- ghan be awarded the merit badge.

The minutes were confirmed: - STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. The committee recommended the payment of accounts. Including £lOO purchase of land from Mr. Biekestaff for street improvement, amounting to £lO3 103. It also recom- mended that the following plans be approved :—Alterations to two houses in Wilderspool-caasewav, for Mr. John Lunt; alterations to house in Latchford. for Mr. Joseph Hall; iron building near Church-street, for Mr. Bower; 14 cottages in Garibaldi-street, for Mr. Edward A. Heckle; twe houses off Knutsford-road. for Mr. Edward Rogers. On the motion of Councillor BROADBENT, seconded by Councillor Dtxox, these minutes were adopted.
SANITARY COMMITTEE -THE TREATMENT OF MEMORIALISTS.

The Sanitary ComMiTt-e-eV-n-a-int-tie; included recommenda- tions for payment of aoctunts (including £450 on contract for depot) amounting to £629 17s lid; and another amount (including £l5O re Lythgoes-lane depot) of £454 9s 81. Alderman BURGESS moved, and Councillor SUTTON seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor MACKIE inquired whether any reply had ever been given by the Sanitary Committee to the memorial pre- wented two months since in connection with the erection of the •arinal in Bnttermarket-straet. The gentlemen who signed that memorial complained that the committee had not, he believed, even recognised their previous memorial. They then presented one direct to the Town Council, which was ruled to be not quite in order, and, as he understood, referred to. the Sanitary Committee. He was not present at the previous meeting of the Council, but be looked at the minutes, and did not see the matter mentioned. He should, therefore, be glad to know if the memorialists were treated with proper courtesy, or if any steps had been taken to re- move what was, witoout exception, the most extraordinary erection in his time. It had been said that a cntain em- peror found Rome of brick and let'. it of marble. but it seemed to be the intention of the Sanitary Committee to leave Warrington well supplied with urinals, for they had no less than four between the corner of the park and the police court, which was certainly not a distance of over half a mile. He strongly approved of the erection of the lamp in Buttermarket•streot, but why it should be surrounded by so objectionable an arrangement he did not know. He should be glad to hear of the committee taking steps to re- move it to Bridge Foot, where the land which was pur- chased for improvements did not cost more than in Batter- market-street. The MAYOR said he did not like to interrupt Couneillor Mackie, but he must remind him that his remarks were out ot order, as the subject was not mentioned in the

minutes. Councillor MACKIE contended that they ought not to be tied down so tightly by the standing orders. rhere had been a great deal too much of that on many occasions, (Hear. hear.) The MAYOR said it was not merely the standing orders, but it was provided by a statutory enactment that a certain course should be pursued in that Council. Alderman BURGESS said he did not know he had anything to reply to. It appeared to him that the minutes as pro- posed to the Council had not met with the slightest opposi- tion, and there had not been a thing said upon which there was any need for him to reply to. He did not care to go into the question raised by Dr. Mackie because, he con- tended, they bad nothing to do with it, and further than that, grave insinuations had pervaded the observations of Dr. Mackie. That was not the first time Dr. Mackie had made use of those ra.narks. The Sanitary Committee were in the habit of treating ptople with the respect they were entitled to, and he repudiated Dr. Mackie's observations on that point. He thought it was an extremely unworthy thing to insinuate that any gentletnen on the Sanitary Com• mittee would treat ratepayers who may send memorials with disrespect. He knew the Sanitary Committee did not do that sort of thing, and he was not disposed to enter into a discussion with the gentleman who raised the discussion. Councillor MACKIE said he had made no insinuation or innuendo. He asked a plain, simple, gentlemanly, English question, as to whether a reply had been given to the me- morialists, and he had failed to get an answer. Alderman BURGESS : Then, sir, \Yr: have had no memorial, and Dr. Mackie knows it. Councillor MACKIE : I do not know it. Alderman linuemss : The Council had a memorial but it never Came to us. Councillor Macitte : Well, let the truth come out; / did not know it. Alderman BURGESS: I say you did, but it will get into your paper, and that is what it is intended for. (Laughter.) Councillor MACKIE most positively repudiated those re- marks. Up to that moment he did not know but that the memorial had been presented to the Committee. He ap- pealed to the Mayor if it was not the decision of the Coun- cil two months ago, and if that was not a reason given for the Council not considering the petition. The MAYOR Said there was undoubtedly a memorial pre- sented to the Council, and he read over every name on it. and, if his momory served him right, it was referred to the Sanitary Committee. His impression was to that effect, and he thought they would hardly deal with :a memorial of that kind in any other way, because it would be disrespect- ful to those who sent it if they did otherwise than send it to the committee which had most to do with the subject it re- ferred to. Councillor BROADBENT said he thought that discussion showed the wisdom of the standing order that they slaould confine their discussion to the subject before them. (Hear,

hear.) Alderman BURGESS said that when the memorial came to the Council it was after the Council had ordered the erec- tion of the urinal in Buttermarket-street,and the urinal was in coarse of erection and nearly completed at the time. The Sanitary Committee had not the slightest power to deal with the matter even if t'Aey had had the disposition. They could not set aside an order of the Council if a thousand memorials had come. Councillor' WatrrLE objected to anything being discussed that was not on the minutes; he had been looking for that for some titn.. (Laughter, and cries of " Out of order.") If he had said any thing about it be would have been shut up at once. (Laughter.) The minutes of the Sanitary Committee were then con- firmed.

The minute, of this committee contained as follows : Report of the Inspestor, that 102 cases had been inquired iuto by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 99 cases for 219 children. That 14 cases were taken before the magistrates, when fines were inflicted in 13 cases and 1 dismissed. Note-36 cases were brought before the com- mittee and dealt with.
Minutes c4nfirmed on the motion of Alderman WEBSTER, seconded by Councillor FLEMING.
MUSBUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTBE.-THR TREE LIBRARY QUESTION.

The above-mentioned committee's minutes contained as follows :—Return for April : Visitors to the museum, 2,965, an increase of 8 per cent compared with April, 1885 ; books issued in reading•room, 1,444, an increase of 16 per cent; books issued to subscribers, 1,662, the same as in April. 1885. Return of the following gifts, for which the thanks of the committee were ordered to be sent to the donors :—From Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society, "Year book of scientific societies" -.Mr. C. W. Sutton, a local pamph- let ; the Librarian, two local pamphlets ; the Liverpool Free Library Committee, catalogue of the reference library, two vole.; Mr. Beamont, Schedule of deeds relating to Rix. ton and Glezebrook ; Mr. Fletcher, Municipal Corporations Directory for 1886 —Minute, that a deputation of six gentlemen waited upon the committee and submitted their views on the subject of abolishing the subscriptions and making the library a free lending library. The committee, after hearing the deputation, informed them that the funds of the institution would not at present permit of such a change, involving as it would, not only an annual loss in voluntary subscriptions, but a greatly increased expenditure in maintaining the institution. ALDERMAN Witssvnt, in moving the confirmation of these minutesosaid they would observe that a deputation had waited upon the Committee and submitted their views in advocacy of making the library a free lending library. Now he must say that the gentlemen who attendee on the Committee were most courteously received and listened to for, he should think, an hour. and the subject had been carefully discussed by the Committee. The Committee had sympathy with the deputation to a certain extent, and they wire sorry they could not come to a resolution satisfactorY to the gentlemen composing the deputation. But it was self-evident to any gentleman who went into the matter that the proposed change would caur. an increased expen- diture, and that it would necessitate the absence of about £l5O a year subscriptions. This would necessitate either the closing of a portion of the institution or the procuring of the amount from some other source; and as there was no other source at present open to the Committee they were obliged to come to the conclusioe recorded on the minutes. Correcrmort Surrox seconded the passing of the militates, and they were then confirmed. THE CEMETERY ccocurrno. The receipts for the past four weeks were £49 10s 2d, bud for the corresponding period last year £54.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 5, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 5, 1886.

MR. CHAMiiERLAIN'S speech on the Home i‘tile Bill has naturally been looked forward k° with special interest; for while it was that he greatly disapprovo of some te,t the features of the scheme it was thought Dat the concessions of the Government illight lead him, at the last moment, to vote ior the Bill on the understanding that it should De re-modelled in an autumn session.. It W°llld seem, from the report of the meeting ef his supporters held on Monday, that he Was in favour of making a protest against the 41easure by marchmg out of the House rather than by voting against it; but rash counsels prevailed; he promised to act With the majority at the meeting; and his BPeech in the House of Ccmmons on Tuesday evening confirmed this decision. We re- gfet, deeply regret, that he should hare Placed himself in what we cannot but re- rd as a false position; for, assuming that `4lle bill is lost, and the Government over- it will be most keenly felt by the hulk of the Liberals of Great Britain that tllle Liberal member for West Birmingham 'S been the means of overthrowing the Illost Liberal Government that this country alas ever known. That LORD HARTINGTON Snollld do this. if necessary, in order to corn- ?ass his ends was a matter of course, because Was a matter of consistency ; it was deman- ued by the out-and-out character of his op- Pr,hsition to the principle of Home Rule. laut it was not required of MR. CHAMBER- !4‘, IN that he should take such an extreme ;LeP. He says—" I have said before, and 4 say it again, give me 'the principle Vtbout the bill, and I will vote for it." his may be taken to mean that he would !4ave had MR. GLADSTONE Withdraw the bill, and substitute an abstract resolution, a Course which might have suited MR. CHAM- RitLAIN. but would not have been satisfac- tory to the people of either Great Britain or Ireland. The Prime Minister went as far in the direction of meeting MR. CHAMBERLAIN aS he could possibly do when he practically affirmed that to vote for the bill was to do no Iflore than to "vote in favour of the estab- tTittnent of a legislative body in Dublin for tte management of affairs specifically and rclusively Irish." lithe member for West Inningham could not accept this view of his Position, it was surely sufficient for him to a bstain from voting at all; he was not called °rl) while accepting a principle, to seek to it a death-blow because of a matter of etail in carrying it out. He has incurred a _terrible responsibility—the responsibility of pitting up the Liberal party at the worst pos- sible time, and in the worst possible way. It is lialulciently distracting to have a commander of °ltn HARTINGTON'S eminence refusing to forward, without having a leader like Mr. AMBERLAIN, who admits that we must go rerward, turning round and making confusion Worse confounded because the plan of action is not to his liking. By way of making this latter point clear, he says—" It is upon the thethod and the plan of the bill that we are going to the country." That may be the issue which the member for West Birmingham sets before•him, but if he thinks it is the issue which t,he country itself will regard as vital, he is labour- 'flg under an extraordinary delusion. The great question, in case of a General Election, ll be wnether Ireland is or is not to have lome Rule. On the one hand, there will be e, Tories, with Lord HARTINGTON and his (7hig following, stoutly opposing any conces- 'loh in the direction of granting legislative 411,thnomy for Ireland: and on the other there be the great bulk of the Liberal party, „ed by Mr. GLADSTONE, and supported by the !rlsh Nationalists, resolute and enthusiastic 1,11 the demand for Home Rule. It will not ue a question merely of "the method and the 131 an ' ; the gr at struggle will be as to the rhnciple ; and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN Will then d himself, we imagine, in a very queer earner. If ire elects, finally, to range him- on the side of the Liberals, he will not be a_ble to do so without feeling that he has rhorced a conflict at the wrong' time ; and if De goes over to the opponents of Home he will stand in the unhappy and un- ;orthy position of an aider and abettor in the ht.terript to crush a principle which he has self publicly advocated. Granted that e bill before the country for the better vernment of Ireland is capable of improve- nent, does anybody suppose that the details the measure are likely to be dispassion- y discussed during the heat and turmoil an election campaign? There will be Plenty of reckless assertion on both sides;

, but it is not in this way that defects in the One of the dames of the Primrose League, clauses of a bill can be remedied. If Mr. Mrs. F. J. Craven, of Brockhampton Park, CHAMBERLAIN is confident that time is on Gloucester, has just been divorced from her his side, and that full and free discussion will husband. Captain Pakenham eloped with her bring the electors round to his way of think- —it is a way they have in the army. The ing, why has he not accepted Mr. GLAD. runaway was faithful to the Primrose League STONE'S suggestion for suspending the bill un- though faithless to her husband, for she sent til the autumn, the interval to be employed in him the key of the drawer which contained influencing public opinion by rrians of the the money of the League. The rest of the platform and the press ? It seems to , Knights and Dames will doubtless be very us that this is exactly what is needed in the proud of the woman who does not cease to interests of those who wish to see the Irish think of them even when she is eloping. question settled on a satisfactory and perma- nent basis. Great progress has been made in ; three months on the Home Rule question; even Mr. CHAMBERLAIN admits the " uni- versalitv and coinpleteness " of the sentiment "in favour of some form of Home Rule for Ireland." Why, then, if the feeling is growing, should he not encourage that growth until he can turn it to .account in remodelling the , measure for an autumn session ? We can understand why the Tories should desire a dissolution at the present moment—they wish ' to snatch a victory whilst the Liberals are in some degree divided; we can understand why Lord HARTINGTON should not be averse to an appeal to the country, seeing, as he does, that to prevent Home Rule for Ire- land he must strike now or never; but we cannot understand why Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, professing, as he does, to accept the prin- ciple of legislative autonomy for Ireland, and believing, as he does, that public opinion is advancing in this direction, should take a course of action which will be hateful to the Irish Home Rulers, which will estrange him from his friends, and make him the laughing-stock of his enemies. Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN is a riddle to us, and, for the present, we must give him up.

The members of the Commission on the :-)eprrssion of Trade are possessed of inquir- ing minds. They have issued a special report on the currency question, which expresses the opinion that the subject is one of great urgency, and recommends that a special body should be appointed to inquire into it. Just so—keep the ball rolling. We may expect a final report on these matters of " great urgency" in a decade or two. Why don't the Fair Traders, who are left in the dark, call on their Commissioners to "hurry up ?'' As things go, the Protectionists may die before they see daylight.

Some discussion took place at the St. Helens Town Council on Wednesday on the course the Library Committee were taking in providing music-cooies of oratorios, &c., to be lent to the public as ordinary books. In the course of the conversation, Councillor Hanson said " the expenditure of the Library had never exceeded a halfpenny in the pound on the rates." Query: If St. Helens can maintain a Free Library with a halfpenny in the pound on the rates, how is it that Warrington cannot make its Library free with a penny in the pound?

What a wretched exhibition of circumlocu- tion —the Warrington Corporation officials compelled—and on a Sunday, too--to cart water to thirsty horses because somebody refuses to supply the animals from a hydrant! We shall hear next, as we did last summer, of workmen toilmg at their various avocations being unable to get a drink of water at the works. Is there no means of bringing to an end the game of cross purposes between the Corporation and' the Waterworks Co. ? Must it go on for ever —a discredit, as the Mayor admits, to the borough ?

DISREGARD for the law amongst Tory law- makers seems to be contagious. Last week • LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL made the at- tempt to justify his incitement to the Orange- then of Ulster to fight, in case they were called upon to send representatives to an Irish Parliament; anci now we have a ' Bishop—a member of the House of Lords— intimating that he will disregard a pat ticular law until it has received the sanction of Con- vocation. On the iSih of May an Act of arliament came irito force, extending the hours during which it is lawful in this coun- try to perform the marriac-e ceremony.. Pre- vious to last month, a marriage could not be solemnised after noon; but the new law ex- tends marriage by license LID to three o'clock in the afternoon. The Bishop of Lichfield, having been written to with respect to a mar- riage which, it was proposed, should take place in the afternoon, sent a reply through his secretary, which is certainly extra- ordinary :—"The Bishop," the secretary says, "does not propose altering the hours in the marriage licenses until the canon law is al- tered by Convocation, so as .to bring it in harmony with the statute law." According to this, the law is not the law until it is ap- proved by Convocation. Queen, Lords, and Commons may pass Acts of Parliament, but they are to be a dead letter until life has been breathed into them by Convocation. But if Convocation is to have this power, why not the Methodist Conference, or a Convocation of the Secularists, or of the Salvation Army? It is true the Bishop talks of bringing the the "Canon law" into harmony with the "Statute law ;" but what if Convocation should prefer the old order of things to the new? And what, meantime, of those who wish to avail themselves immediately of the Statute law? Are they wholly out of Court? It will be interesting to see if any of the Queen's subjects residing in the diocese of Lichfield will contest this new ruling of Dr. Maclagan, and whether any of the other Bishops will follow his example. It is bad enough to have Bishops as law makers in the House of Lords; but it is worse to see them setting aside laws which they have helped to make.

Mr. Chamberlain referred in his speech in the House on Tuesday evening to his specific declaration at Warrington that he would be no party to Mr. Parnell's demands for separation; but who talks of separation? Mr. Chamberlain did not then say, as he says now, that he was in favour of the principle of Home Rule. If he was in favour of tiome Rule when at Warrington, he kept the fact to himself. If he has ad- vanced since then, why should the Liberal Party be accused of inconsistency because they have advanced a little faster than he, and a little further ?

Mr. T. P. O'Connor let the cat out of the bag as to Bolton in his speech on the Home Rule Bill, in the House of Commons, on Thursday evening. It seems that the Tories gave the Parnellites carte blanche as to printing at the last election. It would be in- teresting to know if a similat arrangement was in existence at Warrington. It would account for the profuse display of Mr. Par- nell's Manifesto. Mr. O'Connor says he could "startle the House " if he were at liberty to tell all he knows as to Tories in high position. Pity he is not at liberty to speak out.

Mr. Gladstone, in a letter dated yesterday, and written in reply to a communication from Mr. J. F. Moulton, M.P., reaffirms his state- ments that to vote for the second reading of the Home Rule Bill is to vote only for the principle of the bill ; and that it will be the duty of the Government to consider all pro- posed amendments prior to an autumn ses- sion. The seceders have therefore no loop- hole of escape. if they vote against the bill, they must not afterwards ask their constitu- ents to believe that they approve of its principle.

A RAINIIILL DIVORCE CASE.—In the Probate Divorce, and Admiralty Division, before Mr. Justice Butt, the case of Bull v. Bull was heard. This was a suit by Emily Bull, whose maiden name was Statham, for the dissolution of her marriage with Henry Clay Bull because of his cruelty and adul- tery. Mr. Middleton appeared for the petitioner; there was no defence. The respondent was an American, and had been married and divorced •in America. From the evidence of the petitioner, who is only about 23 years old, and of other wit- nesses, it appeared that the petitioner and the respondent were married on August 30, 1884, at Liverpool. They went to Furness Abbey for their marriage trip, and returned to Liverpool on Septem- ber 6, when they took up their residence at Rainhill. —Evidence was given in regard to the ill-treatment, and in answer to a question from the Judge, Mr. Walker, who had acted as secretary to Mr. Bull, lescribed him as a drunkard. As to the adultery, ividence was given to show that last year a detec- tive, who entered a disorderly house at Liverpool in 4earch of a thief, found the respondent there with a voung woman who was one of the witnesses at the rial.—Mr. Justice Butt pronounced a decree nisi, t with costs.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

It is now proposed that the Home Rule de- bate shotild terminate on Monday night. It must finish sometime, but the most that can be hoped is that it will be brought to an end before the Whitsuntide holidays.

A local contemporary speaks of the Home Rule Bill as "a drowned rat." This is a " neutral " way of putting things—purely neutral of course. But it is better not to pro- phesy ; the "drowned rat" may prove to be a live lion in the path of Tories and Neutrals, and Neutral-Tories. The Manchester Ship Canal Bill passed the second reading in the House of Lords on Monday. It is a good sign that there was no discussion. What is wanted now is action; there has been sufficient talk.

Pick-pockets and card sharpers seem to have been busy at Newton Races. One young man was robbed of a valuable gold watch. Next time he will probably think of the advice given in the following witty couplet : "He who to races goes two things must do— Pocket his watch and watch his pocket too."

The St. Helens Council are now in full possession of the estate which will constitute the Park for the town ; and it is proposed to open the Park on Whit-Monday. It has been resolved to spend about £3,000 in immediate improvements; and, as this will help to brighten and beautify the people as well as the park, it will be money well spent.

The Bishop of Lichfield declines to grant licences under the new Act (which extends the hours of marriage by license) until it has been passed by Convocation. To set aside the law is disloyal; disloyalty is treasonable; treason merits capital punishment. Why then not suspend the Bishop who would sus- pend the law? The rescue of a child at Warrington, on Sunday, from drowning in the Mersey, was gallantly done by Mr. Charles Roddy, who did not hesitate to risk his life in 15 feet of water. "Adventures are to the adventurous." It is stated that this is not the first time he has thus saved life ; and it is to be hoped that application will now be made on his behalf for the medal of the Humane Society.

In contrast with the courage of Mr. Roddy, we have the cowardice of a boatman, or rather a canal "loafer," named James Sum- ner. A child three years of age had fallen into the canal, at Runcorn, and was observed to be floating in the water by Sumner, who, instead of making an effort to rescue, went in search of the dock constable! The child was afterwards got out of the water, but too late to save its life. Sumner, who seems to be "a bit daft," said it would have made him dizzy to attempt to reach the child. He was censured, but it would have 'been no worse if the censure had been followed by a ducking in the canal.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL-At a recent meeting of the Parliamentary Committee of the Liverpool City Council the Town-clerk reported that the special committee of the House of Lords, ap- pointed to consider the question of payment of in- terest out of capital during construction, had de- cided to amend standing order 128 of the House of Lords to make it agree with the standing orders of the house of Commons. Resolved—" That the bill be opposed in committee of the Lords." The Town- clerk requested the instructions of the committee as to the Corporation appearing by counsel before the select committee appointed to consider the bill, and it was resolved—" That Mr. Pope, Q.C., and Mr. Potter, Q.C., be retained as counsel for the Cor- poration." BOWLING MATCH AT DITTON FOR £2o.—On Mon- day afternoon the green attached to the Ball Inn, Ditton, was the scene of a lively contest between two well-known professionals, George Ball, of War- rington, and J. biker, of West Houghton, who had agreed to play a game of bowls, 51 up, for £lO aside. There was a moderate attendance of specta- tors, and the green was in good condition. Ball was favourite at 5 to 4 on, but very little money changed hands. Ball was the first to score, and to- talled 12 to his opponents 4, after which the latter went to 17 to 15, and the pair afterwards peeled at 19 and 24. Holker now put in four points, when Ball commenced to play in fine form, and went rapidly to the front, scoring 33 to 28, 38 to 32, and 39 to 35. At this stage of the game Holker.went off Ins play altogether, and was unable to make any progress, leaving Ball to run out the winner by 16 points. The scores, at the finish Were :—Ball, 51 ; liolker, 35.

Tfric WINDFALL TO LANCASHIRE FAMILIES.— Several Lancashire families as previously reported, have substantiated their Claims to he Harrison estates, the owner of which died intestate at War- rington. The successful claimants are Mr. Thomas Comall Barton, of Bolton; Mary Jane Bulcock, of Preston; Alice Jane Forrest and Louisa Emily For- rest (both infants), of Preston ; and Elizabeth Dob- son, wife of a civil engineer living in Chicago. The property was left by Mr. Richard Harrison, of Lovely-lane, Warrington, who died in 1863 without a will. The successful Bolton claimant, Mr. Thomas Cornell Barton, is an elderly man, and was formerly a Scripture reader at St. Matthew's Parish, Bolton. Mr. Barton did not become acquainted with the case until July of last year, although relatives of Mr. Harrison were repeatedly advertised for. He I then put the matter in the hands of Mr. Jeans, I solicitor, Warrington. Previous to this a cousin of ' Mr. Barton, a Prestoi . gentleman, had endeavoured to establish his claim, through his relationship with a younger branch of the Barton family, to which Mr. Barton, of Bolton, has proved he belongs, but can trace his descent from an elder son. To estab- lish his right the registers of Lea, Penwortham, and other churches in the Fylde district have been ~earched, and Mr. Barton can trace his descent from ancestry as far back, as 1601, when a member of the .Barton family married a Miss Helen Harri- son, a direct ancestor of the Harrison whose in- testacy has caused such prolonged litigation. the I other claimants trace their descent from the Har- rison'side, one of them putting in docurnents so far back as the reign of Henry VIII. Mrs. Slagg, wife of the late M.P. for Manchester, and Archdeacon Harrison were formerly claimants, but they with- drew from the suit, Mr. Barton and his co-claimants paying the costs. The estate is estimated to realise £9OO a year. • A PROFESSIONAL THIEF. -7- At the Warrington Borough Court. on Thursday morning, before Major Litton, a respectably dressed young man named John Martin Meade, last from Belle Vue jail, was charged with stealing from the dwelling-house of , William Draper, 13, Rylands-street, Warrington, on I the 31st July of last year, a silverlever watch, value I £2 10s, the property of Thomas Vost, plasterer, of 2, • Ring-street, Eccles. Chief Constable Hunt said that prosecutor in July last year lodged at the house of Draper, and worked at the alterations at the Public Hall. Prisoner came to Warrington and took lodg- ings on the 30th July at 13, Rylands-st., where he represented himself as being a foreman under. the Government Telegraphic Department who had come to Warrington to do some work. On the 31st July prosecutor left his watch hanging above the mantlepiece in the kitchen, and it was seen by the landlady in the afternoon. Prisoner passed in and out during the day, professing to be waiting for his tools. Both prisoner and the watch afterwards dis- appeared. On the 27th of August following, Chief Constable Hunt received a letter from the (leputy- chief constable of Manchester, saying that there was a man in custody there who, from information received, was a man the Warrington police were in search of on a charge of stealing a watch. It was ascertained that the surmise was right, and pri- soner himself afterwards confirmed it, and said that he had pledged the watch in Dale-st., Liverpool, for 255, on the day of the robbery. On the 29th August he was committed for trial at Manchester, , and on the 3rd September following was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment for stealinc, sewing machines by means of a trick. On his release he was met at the prison gates by Constable Neill, of the Warrington police, and taken into custody. Soon afterwards a Widnes policeman went to the prison with the intention of apprehending prisoner for a robbery. Major Litton committed prisoner to take his trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

DROWNING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.-COWARDLY CtiliDt., CT OF A BOATMAN.

On Tuesday afternoon, at the Vine Hotel, Rancern, Mr. T. J. Ridgway. the coroner, held an inquest on the body of William Silas Wood, three years of age. son of William Wood. a heatinan, who lives in Vine-yard.—From the state- ment of Elizsbeth Lamb, grandmother of the deceased, it appeared that the child was playing near the house +About half-past five. A quarter ef -an hour afterwards he was misted, and shortly before six o'clock she found him float- ing in the Bridgewater Canal, between Waterloo Bridge and Savage's Bridge. A boatman named Nicholls took the body out, and conveyed it home, where Dr. MacLennan did all in his power to restore animation, rho child was not dead when taken home, because after Mr. Moores gave him some brandy he vomited a deal of water.—James Sumner, who said he was a boatman and lived at Acton Bridge, de- posed that about ten minutes to six on Monday night he saw the body of the child in the water. .He did not pull it out because such an attempt would have made him dizzy and light-headed. Instead of doing so or calling for anis- tance, he went to look for the dock constable, who told him te go to the police station.-The Coroner: Did you ever get a A body out of water? No, sir.-Have you ever tried? No, sir.- How do von know that it makes you dizzy then? I have seen them in the water and when I have gone to them it has made me so dizzy that I should have fallen in myself. —But there were people within a few yards, to whom you could have called for assistance? Yes, but I went for the constable —Tbe Coroner said if witness ever saw another body in the water he must not walk away without making an effort to get it out, or call the assiqance of some person elm's to. This child had probably lost its life through him walking away without makieg the effort which he ought to have done. The Corener did not know anything about the ewitness, and was not able to judge whether be was telling the truth, but be doubted very touch whether be was doing so.—Mr. Ftaxishem (a jury. man): I think he deserves censuring. Mr. Moores (another juryman) said the child was certainly alive when taken out of the water, and it was able to swallow brandy. He believed that if the chili had been taken out of the water sooner, the efforts made to restore animation would hive been succ:st,ful.—The Coroner said the slightest effert on the part of Sumner would prebebly have saved the life.—ln reply to the Coroner, P.C. Sutton saiet Sumner was a loafer, but sometimes went with boats for his meet.—The Coroner: Is be •' all there ? "—The Constable: I don't think he is, sir.—The Coroner: I don't think any ba iy, with the feeliogs of a man, would have actai as Sum- ner has done—Mr. S. Yarwoed said his action was that of an ineane m in.—The Coroner said the only teing in Sum- ner's favour was that some people had an uncontrollable dislike to touch dead bodies.—The jury returned a verdict of accidentally drowned, and being unanimously of opinion that Stunner should be censured, the Coroner gave him a severe lecture.—On the proposal of Mr. S. Yarwood, the Coroner presented the fees of theljarymen (12s) to the parents of the deceased, who are ill in bed and in very poor circumstances. Tee Coroner added a shilling.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO MET. JAMES FOLEY, OF
div.p: PRESENTATION TO MET. JAMES FOLEY, OF
WIDNES.

On Thursday eveniag a meeting of the friends and sup- porters of Mr. James Foley, recently the scripture reader at the Widnes Parish Church, wee held in Mali's Temper- ance Hall. The proceedings commenced wi.h a tea, at which about 20 persons were present, one half of whom were of the" fair sex." At the subsequent meeting this number was increased by about five. Mr. Thomas Reay presided. It will be remembard that when Mr. Foley called a meeting a month ago a number of pi-eminent Churchmen attended, stormed the platform, and altogether a scene of greet disorder took place. Mr. Foley and his friends even- tually retired, and left the room in possession of their op- ponents. The chairman on Thursday evening made no re- ference to these proceedings, but spoke in terms of approval of the evangelical services Mr. Foley has lately conducted in the Temperance Hall. Mr. W. J. Rankin, secretary to the "Foley Help Fund," made a speech. He said that at the beginning of February the vicar of Widnes stated before the Bishop of Lietrpool that he had an indefatigable lay rider. going from house to house, but, terangely, he gave Mr. Fohy notice a month after that a atement. A deputa- tion waited upon the vicir to aseertaie the reason for this disinies4, and the rev. eeutlemen's reply was that the par- ishioners had nothing to do with the matter. The vicar, he pointed out, was invited to attend the meeting called a month ago, and this showed that nothing was intended to be said that would net bear the light of day. Many scan- dals hed heal circulated with reference to Mr. Foley. One lof them aria that Mr. Foley had stolen some letters, and a second was thut he had forged the name of the Rev. J. Wright-V‘ Miami. In fact he had heard so many scandals about Mr. Foley that it would take him nearly an hour to relate them. If. however, Mr. Foley had been guilty of the two crimes mentioned it was not three months notice that would have been given him. It was prison. He read a testimonial which had been signed by upwards of 200 in- habitants of the town. It was printed and neatly framed for presentation to Mr. Foley. The testimonial re- ferred to his successful labours during the past two years, and added that this testimonial was to be taken as an indication of the respect and esteem in which Mr. Foley had been held during his residence in Widnes. They had observed his unswerving allegiance to the glorious reformation, and his indefatigable efforts to raise the social, moral, and spiritual welfare of the people. The testimonial was signed by Mr. Rankin and the commit- tee. The speaker then rebuthd some slanders that had been made against his character.—Mr. B. Patin made the presen- tatien, and, alluding to the recent meeting, said he was sur- prised and disgusted that a number of persons setting them- selves up as a body of Christie; men should act in such a. disgraceful manner.—Mr. Foley acknowledged the presenta- tion. During his sojourn in Widnes he had, be said, en- deavoured to do his duty, but he was sorry to say he had been grossly misrepresented. He could only hope that theme persons would repent of their folly and lamest their own rem irks, which he bad for the sae of Christian charity overlooked. He did not intend on the last occasion to say anything which might give the slightest offence. Tne very fact that tbe vicar had been asked to attend was a guarantee that nothing offensive would take place. Lies, he declared, had been disseminated through- out the town, so much so, that large numbers of people had viewed him with the greatest disdain and contempt. He. however, stood before them that night feeling in his con- science that he bad done his duty. His conscience declared him clear. His only object had been to bring the Gospel to the people, irrespective of creed or class. He rejoiced that his efforts had not been in vain.—Messrs. Harrison, J. Ford, and R. G. M McLean also epoke.—Mr. Ford made some very strong remarks upon the conduct of the vicar. —The meeting then concluded with the usual votes of thanks.

div.head: MARRIAGE AT FRODSHAM OF MISS
div.p: MARRIAGE AT FRODSHAM OF MISS

GARNETT. The marriage of Miss Mary Garnett, eldest daugh- ter of Mr William Garnett, of Mickle Trafford, and carrying on business as a cabinet maker at Chester, to Mr. Robert Cathgart Smith, son of Mr. Robert Smith, gentleman, Guilden Sutton, took place in. Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Frodsham, on Thursday morning, in the presence of a large number of spec- tators. The bride is well-known and respected at Mickle Trafford and also at Helsby, where her father formerly resided, and where she engaged in good works for the benefit of those by whom she was surrounded. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a dress of bishop's lawn, a wreath of orange blossoms in her hair, and a tulle veil, and carried a magnificient bouquet. The brides- maids, each of whom carried a basket con- taining white lilacs, were attired in dresses of bishop's lawn, with wreaths of margueri- tes in the hair, and white tulle veils. -Their names are Miss Amy Coop (Southport), Miss Fanny Garnett and Miss Helen Garnett (of Penketh), cousins of the bride; and Miss Alice Garnett (Mickle Trafford), sister of the bride. The best man was Mr. Robert Walton, of Chester and the of- ficiating ministers the Revs. William Jessop, of Rawdon, Leeds, and J. M. Bamford, of Chester. During the service the well-known hymn, "The • voice that breathed o'er Eden," was sung by the congregation, Mr. John S. Rimmer, of ham, a friend of the bride and bridegroom, presiding at the organ. Before the service Mr. Rimmer also played a concerto by Dussek and a symphony from Mozart, and, as the newly-married couple left the church for the vestry, Mendelssohn's "Wedding March" was pealed forth. The register having been signed, the guests left for Mickle Trafford, where the breakfast was provided. The path from the church to the carriages was strewn with flowers; and the newly-married couple, as well as the guests, were treated to heavy showers of rice by some of the spectators. The honeymoon is to be spent at London and Brighton. The wedding presents are both numerous and costly. The guests who attended the wedding included Mr. and Mrs. William Garnett, Mr. Robert Smith, Mr. and Mrs. Robert Garnett (Penketh), Miss Garnett, Mr. and Mrs. Jessop, Mrs. Coop (Southport), Mr. and Mrs. Frank Coop, Mr: and Mrs. Fildes, Mrs. Lowe, Mr. Walton, Mr. John Garnett, Mr. Arthur Garnett (brothers of the bride), Mr. A. Jessop, Mr. Bamford, Mr. Herbert Garnett, and Mr. John S. Rimmer. Triumphal arches had been erected at Mickle Traf- ford and at Guilden Sutton, those at the former place in honour of the bride, and those at the latter in honour of the bridegroom.
