div.head: HOME RULE CRISIS.
div.p: THE HOME RULE CRISIS.

The members of the Bath Liberal Association who do not agree with the Government's Irish proposals have formed a local branch of the Liberal Associa- tion for the maintenance of the legislative union. Mr. L. J. Baker, M.P., in acknowledging a reso- lution passed by the Tiverton-on-Avon Liberals, states that he will be enabled to vote for the second reading of the Home Rule Bill in consequence of the modifications and alterations to be made in the scheme. Professor Ruskin has addressed the following letter to a gentleman in North Wales with reference to the Irish crisis :—" Nothing that any Parliament could do would be of the least use at present. England and Ireland must suffer for their past sins; how long and to what issue heaven only knows." Mr. Michael Davitt, speaking on Saturday, at a crowded meeting at Barrow on Home Rule, said he had repeatedly urged during the past seven years that if the merits of the Irish question were presen- ted to the British public he felt sure they would be willing to confer a great measure of justice upon that country. He was immensely amused at the threatened insurrection in Ulster if the Home Rule Bill was carried. They heard the same threats when the Irish Church was disestablished. Such threats were only deserving of contempt. The following passage expressing the late Mr. Disraeli's views on the Irish question was delivered in the House of Commons on the 16th of February, 1844. It will be read with interest in Conservative circles at the present time :—" I want to see a pub- lic man come forward and say what the Irish ques- tion is. One says it is a physical question, another a spiritual. Now it is the absence of the aristocracy, then the absence of railroads. It is the Pope one day ; potatoes the next. You must consider Ireland as you would any other country, in your closets. .Then you will see a teeming population, which with reference to the cultivated soil is denser to the square mile than that of China, created solely by agriculture. . . . That dense population in ex- treme distress inhabits an island where there is an Establish ed Church, which is not their church ; and a territorial aristocracy, the richest of whom live in distant capitals. Thus you have a starving popula- tion, an absentee aristocracy, and an alien church, and, in addition, the weakest Executive in the world. :This is the Iriih question. Well, then, what would hon. gentlemen say if they were reading of a country in that position? They would say at once the remedy is revolution—and why? Because Ire- land is connected with another and a more power- ful country. Then, what is the consequence? The connection with England thus becomes the cause of the present state of Ireland. If the connection with England prevents a revolution, and a revolution is the only remedy, England logically is in the odious position of being the cause of all the misery in Ire- land. What, then, is tlni duty of an English Minis- ter? To effect by his policy all those changes which a revolution would do by force That is the Irish question in its integrity. . . The moment you have a strong executive, a just ad- ministration, and ecclesiastical equality, you will have order in Ireland."

Mr. T. A. Dickson, late member for Tyrone, waited upon Mr. Gladstone on Monday morning to present I him with a letter supporting the Premier's Home Rule proposals signed by 500 Liberal Protestants in Belfast and the counties of Antrim and Down. These signatures, Mr. Dickson stated, were collec- ted in a few days, and more than a thousand addi- tions would shortly follow. Mr. Gladstone expres- sed himself much pleased to receive this expression of Liberal Protestant opinion from Ireland. "Restoration Day" was on Saturday signalised at Grocers' Hall. London. by the admission of the Marquis of Salisbury to the honorary freedom of the company. A banquet was subsequently held in the large hall of the company, under the presi- dency of the Master. To his right sat the Marquis of Salisbury, on his left Lord John Manners. Those present included Sir R. A. Cross, Lord Halsbury, Viscount Cranborne, M.P., Lieut.-General Lord Chelmsford, Sir James Paget, Bart., &c. —The Master proposed, "The Health of our Brother Grocer, the Marquis of Salisbury," and presented him with the freedom of the company.—Lord Salis- bury, in responding, referred to the political situa- tion. He remarked that they were often told that Pitt carried the union between England and Ire- land by bribery. If that was true in any sense, it would be much more true, if that Union is shattered, that its death will be due to unscrupulous intimida- tion. They saw one body of men promoting a cer- tain policy with the conviction that it will lead to separation, and another body promoting it on the assured ground that it is the only way to prevent separation. Opinions may be right, or they may be wrong, but it was certain that one party was being bamboozled. But while Parliament was manceuvr- ing, what was the effect of its action on the coun- try which was principally concerned—lreland? What had been done was this—that whereas if the bill had been passed on with all celerity and with- out any devices to prolong the debate, it might have received a decisive judgment, either from the House of Commons or the House of Lords, in the course of the next month or two. And if that judgment was

unfavourable, the opinion of the people of Great Britain might have been ascertained. Until the opinion of the people of Great Britain had been as- certained, there was no surety, no security, no prosperity possible to Ireland. (Cheers.) Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M P., telegraphing to the "Freeman's Journal," on Tuesday, says :—Things look very bad for the second reading of the Home Rule Bill. He holds that defeat may be a blessing in disguise, and professes anxiety to know what the constituencies will say. On Tuesday morning Mr. Schnadhorst left Bir- mingham for London to watch the progress of events. News of the decision of Mr. Chamberlain's meeting produced a profound sensation at the Birmingham Liberal Club. Mr. Rathbone, the Liberal member of the Arvon Division of Carnarvonshire, has issued a pamphlet to every elector explaining the cause of his antag- onism to the Home Rule measure. A strong feeling exists in the constituency because of Mr. Rathbone's opposition to the Premier, and disapproval has been freely expressed. On Tuesday, at the Irish National League meet- ing in Dublin, the receipt of .EBOO from Sydney was announced. Mr. Dawson said the rejection of the second reading of the Home Rule Bill would lead to a larger measure. He disapproved retaining the Irish members at Westminster. At a banquet given by the City Conservative Club in London on Wednesday night, Lord It. Churchill was the guest, and he made a speech upon the political situation. He had always believed in the absolute impracticability of any repeal move- ment, and in the insolubility of the Home Rule question. The duty of the Tory party in this tre- mendous crisis was to preserve the empire, and that could best be done by cherishing and protecting the independence of the Ilouse of Commons. LETTER FROM MR. BRIGHT.

Mr. Bright has written the following letter to Mr. Grosvenor Lee, of Birmingham :—" Reform Club, May 31, 1886.—Dear Sir,—Forgive me for not hav- ing replied sooner to your letter. The debate will soon close, and there will be time to discuss the bills after they are withdrawn. I think the Home Rule Bill should have been withdrawn before the second reading, and but for the fear of dissolution which decides the votes of some scores of members this would have been done. I hope the course I shall take will meet with the approval of those I am per- mitted to represent. At some not distant day I shall seek the opportunity of discussing the whole lrish government question in your Town Hall. My sympathy with Ireland, north and south, compels me to condemn the proposed legislation. I believe the united Parliament can and will be more just to all classes in Ireland than any Parliament that can meet in Dublin under the provisions of Mr. Glad- stone's bill. If Mr. Gladstone's great authority were withdrawn from these bills, I doubt if twenty mem- bers outside the Irish party would support them. The more I consider them, the more I lament that they have been offered to Parliament and the coun- try.* NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.

A meeting of the General Committee of the Na- tional Liberal Federation was held on Wednesday at the Westminster Palace Hotel, "for the purpose of receiving the resignation of the officers who dif- fered with the decision of the recent meeting of the Federation to form an emergency committee and help forward the promotion of a special fund to promote the policy of federation." Mr. James Kit- son, of Leeds, president, occupied the ch ir, and there was a large attendance. •Mr. Schnadhorst read letters from Mr. William Harris, chairman of committee, Mr. J. T. Bunce, Mr. Richard Chamber- lain, M.P., Mr. William Kendrick, M.P., Mr. J. Powell Williams, M.P., and Dr. Crosskey. The several members regretted that, after the action of the Council in rejecting the advice of the officers of , the Council at the recent meeting, they felt they had no course but to resign, and they did so with deep regret. The Chairman expressed no-I-et that these resignations were to take place, but he felt

div.head: EXAMINER* S A.TURDAY, JUNE 5, 1886
div.p: THE EXAMINER* S A.TURDAY, JUNE 5, 1886

sure that that the action taken by the Council was the proper one, and that was proved by the number of associations now wishing to join them, as shown by their proceedings. Mr. Jesse Collings said it was a sad crisis in the history of the Federation ; and amidst considerable interruption declared that those who were opposed to the bill had not de- gerted their great leader. The resignations were ultimately accepted.

The Press Association says :—A five-lined whip was issued to the Conservative members on Thurs- day morning requesting their attendance on Friday night, for the division on the Rome Rule Bill. At the monthly meeting of the Metropolitan Rad- ical Federation, held on Wednesday night at th• Blouses Club, Chelsea, at which twenty-one Lbndon clubs were represented, a resolution was passed urg- ing all lovers of liberty to stand by Mr. Gladstone in his attempt to pass a measure establishing a Par- liament in Dublin.

Mr. Caine, the Whip of the Chamberlain group, says that the Liberal opponents of the Home Rule Bill who are certain to vote against it number 88. The hon. member for Barrow suggests that Mr. Gladstone should withdraw the bill and proceed by a resolution simply affirming the principle of an Irish Parliament for domestic affairs. Such a reso- lution would reunite the Liberal party and be carried by a majority of over 100. The Llandudno Liberal Association and other political bodies in North Wales have addressed a letter to the Premier, informing him that a general election in the summer months would mean ruin to many of the inhabitants of watering-places, and would arouse irritation and hostility against the Govern- ment. At a meeting, on Thursday, of delegates from the Liberal associations in the South Molton division of Devonshire, a resolution was agreed to expressing confidence in Mr. Gladstone and declar- ing that Lord Lymington had ceased to represent the Liberals of the division. "United Ireland" thinks that an outbreak of Irish petulance is the only thing which can endanger Mr. Gladstone's triumph at the polls. DECkION OF CHAMBERLAINITES AGAINST THE

THE SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A WARRING-TON POLICEMAN. At the Liverpool Assizes, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Grantham, two prisoners committed for trial at Warrington on a charge of murderously assaulting a borough policeman in a busy thoroughfare of the town, in open daylight, on the afternoon of Satur- day, the 6th of February last, came up for trial. The two prisoners, Michael Connor (28), labourer, and Michael Hennessey (28), labourer, were indicted for haying attempted to murder Michael Hennessey, a police-constable, and also for having feloniously assaulted hits with intent to do him grievous bodily harm.—Mr. Hope prosecuted, and Dr. Commins and Mr. Segar appeared for the defence.— From the evidence it appeared that at half-past five o'clock on the day in question Police-constable Henneseev and Police-constable Singleton I% ere on duty at the Market-gate, Warrington, when the prisoners came up on the other side of the road. They were making use of bad language, and the constables cautioned them to use better language. Upon this one of the prisoners moved back as if to kick the prosecu- tor, and the latter thereupon gave him a push, which knocked him down. The prisoners upon this moved away, and were followed by the two constables. Wenneseey was heard to say, "I'll well settle vou before I go to sleep." The prosecutor then went to hie beat, and the prisoners returned about half an hour afterwards, when Connor said, "What did I say when I passed a short time ago?" and the prosecutor said he would tell him at the right time. Upon this the prisoner Hennessey caught hold of him by the . leg and Connor struck him on the head with a poker which he bad concealed in his sleeve. The prosecutor was stunned by the blow for a time, and on recovering he heard Conner Isay to Henn es sey, " You draw up and do the mama." He drew his staff and blew his whistle for assistance, upon which two other policemen ran up, and the prismere ran away. His helmet was broken by the force of the blow, and he sustained a wound on his head and lost a deal of blood. The medical evidence showed that had the constable not had on his helmet the blow which he received would pro- bably have been fatal.—lt was urged for the defence that Constable Hennessey in the first place committed illegal acts by Knocking prisoner Hennessey down before he had com- mitted any offence. The dignity of the officer, it was re- marked, had been ruffled by being called a " slop " by the prisoners, and he thought upon that he was justified in committing an illegal act. The prosecutor, when he met the prisoners a second time, again assaulted Hennessey by push- ing him, and it was then that Connor struck him on the head with the poker. As regarded the prisoner Hennessey, he offered no violence to the prosecutor whatever, and was no party to tbe assault which was committ-d. The jury found Connor guilty of attempted muruer, and Hennessey of wounding with intent to do grievous bealily harm. His Lordship, in passing sentence, said Connor had been in prison some twenty-two times for offences of a similar char- acter, and it was evident that he would go on from bad to worse. The case, as regarded him, was hopeless, and all he could do was to protect the public and the police from such men as he. He would have to go to penal servitude for ten years. With regard to Hennessey, it was not evident that he intended to murder the constable, and the jury had taken a merciful view of it. He had been in prison for offences al- most as often as Connor. He would have to undergo five years' penal servitude.
PRESCOT.

VISIT To TH2 EXHIBITION.—Ort Tuesday about 50 per- sons in connection with the church sewing class and mothers' meeting had, through the kindness of the Vicar, their annual treat—this time to the Liverpool Exhibition They wale accompanied by the Rev. H. A. and Mrs. MacNaghton and other ladies and gentlemen, and a very pleasant afternoon was spent. A DnenaTurt.—At the Prescot Pe'ty Sessions, on Tues- day, George Wm. Penfold was charged with deserting from the 28th Lancashire Fusiliers, stationed at Bury. P.S. Bull stated that on the previous evening he met the pri- soner walking through Prescot. On asking him for his , " pass" prisoner produced one which expired early on Monday morning. He was ordered to be imprisoned until an escort arrived.

Tin R SUPPORT OF A FATHER.—JOhe Mullen, a chemical labourer at Widnes, was summoned at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, for neglecting to contribute to an order directing him to pay is per week towards the &Ippon of his father, chargeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr. John Scannell, relieving officer, said the order was made on Feb- ruary 2nd, and the defendant had only paid 3s. The ar- rears amounted to £1 118 &l.—An order for payment was made.

A DISTIIBBADICE.—At the Petty Sessions on Tuesday Ann Gilgannon was summoned for assaulting Margaret Devine, on the 10th ult., in a court off Tea-street, Prescot. Com- plainant stated that defendant dragged her to the floor, and her child was trampled upon and bruised in the scuffle. A witness named Muiley said both parties are alike, one be. in as bad as the other. There was a cross-summons against Devine for using defamatory language. The magistrates dismissed both cases.

Annual, Teter.—On Wednesday the children connected with the Church of England Band of Hope had their annual trip to flew Brighton. About 150 of them left Present at 9•22, arriving in New Brighton about 11 o'clock. A sub- stantial dinner and tea were provided for the young folks to which they did ample justice. The children were accom- panied by the Rey. F. R. Lee and several ladies and gentle- men. The return journey was commenced about half-past six o'clock, after having a most enjoyable day. Pansccrr LOIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of the Prescot Local Boerd was held on Wednesday evening, when there were present—Messrs. C. Spencely (chairman), T. S. Preston, T. P. Hewitt, J. Berrey, J. K. Slack, W. Hatton, H. Whitfield, J. Cowherd (assistant clerk), W. Goldsworth (surveyor), Dickinson (sanitary inspector), and Bixter (rate collector.) Mr. Whitfield moved " That the comiection which at present exists between the ashpits and main sewers in cur Looal Board district is not conducive to the health of the inhabitants, and that with the view of lessening tke present death rate the ashpits be disconnected with the main sewers." This motion gave rise to a lengthy discus- sion, during which the surveyor pointed out that they could not introduce either the pen system or water closets in Prescot without an enormous expense, and he intimated that they were remedying the occasional offensive smells as quickly as possible. The motion was not seconded.ln reply to a question by Mr. Hewitt, the Surveyor stated that What was called Slutch-row in Warrington-road, and the crossing at the bottom end of Kemble st. were to be repaired during the coming menth.—Mr. Berrey gave notice that at the next meeting of • the Board he would move that any member of the Board in speaking to a resolution should rise to his feet, instead of remaining in his seat as at present. FIINBRAL OF Poucrt SEIZOBANT l'ouxrr.—A large gathering took place on Wednesday afternoon, when the Mortal remains of William Pollitt, a genial and much respected officer, were interred in the Cemetery adjoining the Parish Chnrch. The funeral cortege left his late resi- dence shortly before two o'clock. The polished oak coffin, with black mountings, was covered with xrreathe ; the hel- met and belt being also laid on it. The band of the 21st L.R.V preceded, and played the "Dead March" in "Saul." Following were the widow and brother, Mr. Edward Pollitt, and other relatives, and a number of the townspeople, amonget whom were Dr. Green, Messrs. J. Beesley, W. Hatton, R. Charles, H. Durant, H. Makin, C. Wilson, and others. The police of the Prescet Division, numbering over 40, with crape armlets, came next, including Superintendent Barker, Inspectors Wood (Widnes) and Mayoh (Woolton), Bergeants Ball and Charnley (Prescot), Robinson and Clarkson (Widnes), Crawford (Woolton), Strickland (Old Swan), Murphy (Wayertree), Edgar (Huvton), and Coutts (Ditton). Six comrades of his own rank were the bearers The procession was met at the church gate by the Vicar, Rev. H. A. Macnagh ten, who conducted the service in an Impressive manner. The ohurch and its precincts were crowded. The organ assisted in the mournful service under Mr. Newling. The deceased was 44 years of age, and suc- cumbed to an attack of bronchitis after a few days illness on Saturday last, and leaves a widow and two children. He had been a member of the police force for the past fifteen years, five years as sergeant in Prescot and Widnes. Pre- viously he served for twelve years in the Royal Artillery, a part of the time under the East India Company, and was a member of the band. About his last services were ren- dered on the occasion of the recent visit of Her Majesty the Queen to Liverpool, and it is feared that he caught a cold which aggravated the affection to which be had been subject.

P-RBSCOT HIGHWAY BOARD.—The monthly meeting of the Prescot Highway Board was held on Tuesday fere:loon; present—Messrs. W. L.Evens, J.P. (chairman), M. Lowe, J. Newton, J. e4umner, H. A. D'a Willis, J.P. (ex-officio), W. Goldsworth (surveyor), and H. Cross (clerk. 1-1 he Chair- man, in returning thanks for his appointment as chairman for the present year at the last meeting, said he would do his best to promote the interests of the Board, and he hoped they would go on during the year as they had done in the past, in an agreeable manner.—Mr. Lowe also acknowledged the compliment, and thanked them for appointing him vice-chairman—The Steam Road Roller : The Surveyor drew attention to the difficulty of supplying the steam roller with water and coal when in outside districts where there happened to be no water company, and suggested that a lurry with a galvanised iron tank sh mid he obtained, upon which both water, coal, LT., could be placed. This lurry could be affixed to the engine, and thus horse labour would be saved. It was ultimately decided to leave the matter in the hands of the Surveyor and Mr. Newton.—The Expendi- ture: The Surveyor's statement of expenditure for the four weeks ending May 27th was as follows :—Bold £lB 4s 54, Knowsley £8 15e Rainhill £l9 4s 9d, Whiston £l9 4s Id, team labour £44 38 6cl. new materials £46 17s id, incidentals £2 19s 7d, total £159 8s 141. Water Pipe Laying at Knowsley: A letter was read from Mr. Hale, agent to Lord Derby, stating that the St Helens Corpora- tion would shortly commence the laying of pipes for Lord Derby from their new pumping station to the village at Knowsley. He desired to know if the Highway Board had any objection to the roads being taken up for the purpose of laying down and maintaining the pines.—The Surveyor said the Corporation of St. Helens laid down a quantity of pipes lately under certain regulations, and he suggested the same regulations skiuld be made in that case, and that the work should be done to the satisfaction of the waywarden and himself. The course was adepted.—This was the only business of interest.

div.head: BILL.
div.p: BILL.

Excitement in the lobby of the House of Commons reached a climax on Monday evening, when it was ad. mitted that the fate of the Home Rule Bill depended on the decision of Mr. Chamberlain and his friends. A meeting of these gentlemen had been called by means of a circular. which invited those to attend who, being in favour of some form of autonomy for Ireland, disapproved of the Gov2rnment'e bi!ls in their present shape. Fifty-four mem- bers accented the invitation, amongst them being between 15 acd 20 Liberals who are to some extent identiied with Lord Hartington's views; having attended at Devonshire Huse and in other ways shown their sympathy with his lordship.

Mr. Chamberlain presided at the conference, and there were alto preitent Messrs. Trevelyan, Heneage, Caine, Richard Chamberlain, Finlay, David Davies, Sir Joseph Pease, Sir Julian Goldsmid, Sir Hussey Vivian, Mr. Powell Williams, Mr. Saunders, Mr. Mqver, Lord Lymington, Messrs. Cuthbertson, Quilrer, J. Wilson (Edinburgh), Mac- lagan, Mitchell-Henry, A. Browne, Boyd Kinnear, P. Rylands,. Sir H. Havelock-Allan, and Mr. Otter.

'The Chairman said he had received a letter from Mr. Bright, who expressed strong disapproval of the Home Rule Bill, and stated his intention of voting against the second reading. (The reading of the letter caused much enthu- siasm. and the opinion expressed by Mr. Bright had a pal- pable and immediate effect on the meeting.). lhere were only two alt N-natives open to them—to walk out of the House in sufficient numbers to make an imposing demon- stration, and abstain from voting altogether; or to go into the division lobby against the bill. Mr. Chamberlain gave the impression that personally he would prefer to abstain. He threw himself entirely on the meeting, however, declar- ing that whatever course they chose to adopt, if a decision were arrive l at with tolerable accord, he would be bound by it.

An animattd dismission ensued. Several speake,s were inclin,d to abstain from voting, but the majority held that there was no middle course, and that the voting should either be for or against the bill. Mr. Trevelyan, who shared the'latter view, submitted that active opposition was not only the logical but also the only honest course open to them. Sir J. Pease endeavoured to throw oil on the troubled waters by a conciliatory speech, in which he urged upon his hearers the necessity of discussing the subject with moderation and discretion. The hon. baronet, however. soon convinced himself that the sense of the meeting was against further delay, and finally decided to act with the majority. On a vote being taken, it appeared that three of the mem- bers present had keen satisfied by Mr. Gladstone's modifica- tions and were now prepared to vote for the bill, 12 ap- proved of abstaining altogether from voting, whilst 38 were in favour of voting against the second reading. The pre- vailing opinion of the meeting h -tying been thus shown to be decidedly in favour of voting against the bill, another division was agreed upon with a view to ascertain whether, under the circumstances, a common plan of action could be found. The result was that 46 decided to vote against the bill, 4to abstain, and 3to support the Government. One member walked out before the voting took place, not being willing to pledge himself to the course suggested. The meeting commenced at five o'clock and lasted until twenty minutes to seven. LORD HARTINGTON AND TELE LIBERAL UNIONISTS.

The Central News says a meeting of the Hartington group of Liberal ditsidents was held on Tuesday afternoon in one of the Cenference Rooms at the House of Commons, under the presidency of the Marquis of Hartington. There was a full attendance, but it was noticed that several gentlemen who attended the Chamberlain meeting on Monday were else present upon this occasion. There was indeed nothing in the circular of Invitation issued by his lordship to pre- clude their attendance, which was requested "for the pur- pose of considering the action to be taken on the second reading of the Government of Ireland Bill." Lord Har- tington did not arrive until most of his friends had as- sembled. On entering the room he was received with loud cheers, which were repeated when be took the chair. There were then present about 60 Liberal memtere of Parliament, including Sir Henry James, Sir John Ramsden, Sir A Fair- bairn, Colonel Seeley, Sir J. Pease, Baron F. de Rothschild, the Marquis of Stafford, Sir W. Crossman, Sir H. Havelock- Allen, Sir John Jenkins, Sir John Lubbock, and Messrs. Heneage, Rylands, Mitchell Henry, Goschen, Bartley, Fin- lay, A. Brown, A. Elliott, A. Grey, Craig, Seller, H. Brand, J. Maclver, Jrc. The proceedings were opened by Lord Hartington, who explained that the meeting had been called in accordance with an understanding come to at the Devonshire House conference that the party should have another opportunity of discussing the situation previous to the division en the Irish Government Bill. In his lordship's opinion, nothing had occurred in the interval to change the position materi- ally, or to induce them to recede from the attitude they had originally assumed in this matter. Certainly the fea- tures of the Government policy had not been improved by the Foreign Office manifesto, which, if anything, bad made matters worse. The noble Marquis then proceeded to refer to the so-called concessions made by Mr. Gladstone, especially criticising the proposal for effecting a spas- modic representation of Ireland at Westminster—an experi- ment which he was sure would prove ineffective. He thought they would agree with him that the principle for which they contended would not be secured by the new arrangement suggested by the Government. They must also remember that in addition to the difficulty connected with the 24th clause, there were other -objectionable features of the bill, which had not, so far, been touched by a com- promising hand. Therefore it seemed to him that every- thing tended to make their position on this question as cleat as it was when they first met. They were now upon the eve of the division, and in respect to their action in con- nection therewith there were courses open to them. First, to vote against the bill; second, to vote in favour of it; third, to abstain from voting altogether He did not wish personally to influence the minds of his friends, and therefore he should proceea to take a division on each course. His Lordship, amid much cheering, then put the question that the party should vote against the second reading of the Government of Ireland Bill, and, with three exceptions, every hand in the room was held up in its favour. Even the three gentlemen who abstained from voting did so, it was understood, because they had already pledged them- selves to a similar course of action at the Chamberlain meeting on Monday. The noble Chairman, as a matter of from, took the sense of the meeting on the alternative courses, but not one hand was held up for either. There- upon the Chairman declared that the meeting had unani- mously decide 4 to vote against the second reading.

A petition is being signed by members of the Liberal Hundreds in the Rossendale Division, requesting the Liberal Executive to call a meeting of the whole of the members to take into consideration the present crisis respectirg the repre- sentation of this division, and to test the feeling of the Liberal party as to what are the chances Lord Hartington will have in securing his re-election for this division should be offer himself for re-election.

PRINCE GEORGE.—Thursday was the twenty-first anni- versary of the birth of his Royal Highness Prince George Frederick Ernest Albert, K.G , the younger son of their Royal Highnesses the Prince and Princess of Wales, and brother of Prince Albert Victor.

THE HYDE TRAGEDY.—An inquest was held at Hyde, on Monday, touching the death of Mary Knott, wife of Charles Knott, stripper and grinder, of Back Vernon-street, Hyde, and John, his infant son, aged ten months, who were fiainn dead in bed on Thursday night week. After hearing evidence, the Coroner said the presence of strychnine in the stomach of the deceased, and the purchase of a packet of vermin killer the same morning, was sufficient to account for the cause of death, and, therefore, the only verdict the jury could return was one of wilful murder against Mary Knott—for destroying her infant—after which she com- mitted suicide, and there was no doubt from the evidence that at the time she did so she was Of unsound mind.— The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the coroner's suggestion.—On the suggestion of Dr. side- botbatn, the jury made a presentment against the selling of packets of vermin-killer containing such large quantities of strychnine.

div.head: SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GOOD TEMPLARS.
div.p: SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GOOD TEMPLARS.
DISTRICT LODGE AT EA.RLESTOWN.

The quarterly session of the South-west Lanca- shire District Lodge of Good Template was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Cross lane, Arlestown, on Saturday afternoon. There was a very large atten- dance of delegates from South-west Lancashire Dis- trict, and Bro. J. W. Hall, of Warrington. D.0.T., who presided, was supported by all the district officers. A large number of visitors from Widnes, St. Helens, Warrington, Wigan, and other places, were also present, including Brother J. P. Tolton, D.0.T., of the South-east Lancashire District, Bro. William Parncutt, P.W.D C., of Middlesex Dietrict, &c. After the opening ceremonies and the roll call, the D.C.T. (Brother Hall, Warrington) read his re- port for the past quarter, in which he stated that in his visits to difarent lodges be found no despondent spirit pre- vailing, and wherever such a spirit might have been looked for, he had found the cpposite. Many causes told against the progress of their work, and many lodges la- boured under difficulties that were somewhat hard to sur- mount, but none laboured under any difficulty which with perseverance and steady pushing work might not be sur- mounted. He was glad to find in many lodge reports ac- counts of good work done and earnest promises of good work in the future. He urged upon them it was their duty to strive to their utmost to reduce the evils of the drink traffic, and show to the public at large that the work is which they were engaged should go on and prosper. He impressed upon them that much good might be done if the good templar lodges had more outside work and held occa- sional meetings in the open air. There was nothing con- nected with their good work of which they might feel ashamed, and he hoped each lodge would do what it could to make itself successful and strong. He hoped that meet- ing might be a dawning of a bright and glorious future for their work and noble order in the district, and he asked their aid in making that a happy and profitable session. The report of the W. District Secretary (Bro. Morris Jones) showed the taxes and returns from all the ledges in the ,District, and that there had been an increase of one lodge during the quarter, making the total 6,5, with about 2.800 members. The District Treasurer's (Bro. J. J. Wright) showed the finances to be in a fair condition, and the report of the District Electoral Superintendent (Bro. J. Pickersgiil) referred to electoral work during the quarter, in which the members had been actively engaged. The total number of members last quarter was 2,065. initiated 208, total 2,273, while there bad been 218 suspensions and re- movals during the quarter. The average attendance at the lodges had been 920, and one new temple had been initiated at tiarston, which commenced with 19 members and had been increased to 90 He earnestly appealed for the adult members to lend their sympathy and support to the juven- ile temples.—Brother Morris Jones next read the report of the Executive, which alluded to the various meetings held, and the questions they had had under consideratice. Other reports of a minor character were considered, and they were all adopted. Brother George Clarke, D.C., gave a report upon the credentials of representatives and visitors present. After some discussion in regard to the place of meeting for next quarter's session, it was decided to hold the session at Hindley. - -

The following resolution was also passed :—" That seeing the good of our Order, and the advancement of temperance principles, devolves in a great measure on public teraper- ance work, this District Lodge asks its Executive to arrange for a series of open-air public temperance meetings in this district during the summer months." Cordial votes of thanks were paid to the Earlestown friends for their arrangements, and to the visitors, and Brother Geo. Clarke (Earlestown) and Brother William Parnautt (London) re- sponded. This concluded the session.

TEA MEWING. The members and friends afterwards eat dnwn te an excellent tea in the lower schoolroom. About 120 persons attended. A procession was afterwards formed, and an ex- cellent demonstration was made. First was the new banner belonging to the Hope of Earlestown Lodge. and then fol- lowed the Lowton Temperance Brass Band, under the con- ductorship of Mr. John Ashton. Tne district officers and delegates, and other friends, next followed in order, as arranged by Bro. J. Oliver (Liverpool), District Marshall. As the officers and members wore their insignia and regalia, their appearance was very attractive. They marched along Bridge-street, Earle-street, Wellington-street, Rathbone- street, Legh-street, Market-street. and back to the school- room by Bridge-street. A public meeting was afterwards bold in the Wesleyan school under the presidency of the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, of Earlestown, who was supported by Brother J. B. C3llings, G.W.S. (Liverpool), Brother Morris Jones, W.D S., Brother Wm. Parncutt (London), Sister A. M. Green, P.R.W.8.J.T., /sc. The proceedings were commenced with a hymn, after which Brother Morris Jones, W.D.S., offered up prayer. A choir of local members, under the conductorship of Brother George Clarke, W.D.C., next sang the melody " See our. ranks," accompanied on the harnonium by Mr. John El. Profit.—The Chairman said he was not a member of the order, but he had been connected with a lodge at Douglas, and he had very pleasant recollections of its work and in- fluence. He could not disguise from himself a disposition to express a sense of the pain experienced by himself in connection with the recent debate on the Durham Sunday Closing Bill. He confessed that never bad he been more deeply pained than in reading the discussion in the House of Lords, which ultimately resul- ted in the overthrow of that measure. He com- mented at some length upon the speech of Lord Salisbury, maintaining that the people of Durham and their Parliamentary representatives were strongly in favour of the Durham Sunday Closing Bill. He held that the House of Lords had no right to reject it after it had passed every stage except the third reading in the House of Lords. (Applause.) A choir of members of the Pride of Earleatown Juvenile Temple, lead by Brother George Clarke, then sang a melody, entitled "The army of the brave." Sister A. M. Green, P.R.W.S J.T., afterwards addressed the meeting en personal responsibility in the work, and the adult choir, conducted by Brother George Clarke, afterwards sang the .melody, "Come ye, and join our army." This had been specially written for the occasion by Brother George Clarke. Brother J. B. Collings, G.W.S., of the Grand Lodge of England, gave an impressive address, after which the adult choir sang "Good night." The meeting closed with the Benediction.
CHEAPEST HousE in the city for Glass, China, Oriental Wares, and Fancy G00d5.-175, Oxtord-street, Manchester.— ildrt.

A bill has been preplred by Messrs. Bart, A. William, W. Cook, and Robson, M.P.'s, for submission to Parliament, to exempt from the laws of distress for rent the tools and implements of working men, and wearing apparel or bedding to the value of £5.

Two women, named Catherine Smith and Mary Roberts, were committed to the assizes to take their trial, by Mr. Reifies, on Thursday, at the Liverpool Police Court, on a charge of having attempted to procure for immoral pur- poses a girl 16 years of age. Tits Driatm CesB.—The London correspondent of the "Dublin Express" says :—'An application Is to be made in.open court, on Tuesday next, In the Dilke divorce case. The object, I hear, is to allow him to appeal in the interven• tion of the Queen's Proctor."

div.head: E ARLESTOWN.
div.p: E ARLESTOWN.

A GOLD WATCII STOLEN.—A young man, named Rd. Morris, employed at the Viaduct waggon works, had a valu- able gold watch extracted from his pocket while standing in a crowd watching same slight disturbince n-.ar Mr. Wm. Mailing's, New Market Inn, Market-street, Earlestown, on Tuesday night. The small ring by which the watch was attached to the chain was found to have been broken.

SERMONS AT WARGRATE.—The anniversary services in aid of the Wargrave and Vulcan Schools were preached in Emmanuel Church, Wargrave, by the Rev. John Davies, B.A.,curate of Lockwood, and formerly a pupil at the War- grave School, and in the afternoon the same rev. gentleman dElivered an address to the children. The church was ciowded at each service,and the collections throughout the day reached the sum of £2l Ss.

NBw-TON CHURCH Caorn —The choir of St. Peter's Church, Newton, held their annual picnic on Saturday. The members proceeded to Liverpool in a special carriage attached to the 8-50 train from Newton }ridge. On their , arrival they went to the river, and embarking on board one of the ferry steamers, paid a visit to the steamer Great Eastern, now lying in the river. After an inspection they returned to Liverpool and partook of dinner at the Bear's Paw Hotel. They afterwards proceeded to the International kxhibitien, where the remainder of the day was spent, the ' return journey to Newton being made about 10 o'clock. after a most enjoyable out. I THE SHOCEING OUTRAGES AT EABLESZOWN.—At the Liverpool Assizes, on Friday. Robert Jones (16), labourer, pleaded guilty to having, at Earlestown, on the 1941 a Janu- ary last, indecently and feloniously assaulted his sister Elizabeth, a girl under the age of 13 years. His lordship, in passing a sentence of twelve months' imprisonment, said he was sorry he could not order the prisoner to be fl)gged. Why the law allowed those who were a day under and for- bade those who were a day over 16 to he flogged with a birch rod he could not understand. If the prisoner had been sober when he committed the assault he would have sent him to penal servitude.--Charles Eaves (15), labourer, con- victed on an indictment charging him with having. at Val- can, on the 2nd May, feloniously assaulted Isabel St urgess, a girl under the age of thirteen, was sent to gaol for one month, and ordered to receive twenty strokes with a birch rod. ; DARING ROBBERY OF £3 AT EARLESTOWN.—One of • the most impudent and daring robberies it is possible to imagine was committed in the dining room of Mrs. John- • eon's shop, Market-street, Earlestown, on Wednesday after- noon. The races at Newton Common are known to attract a large number of the light fingered gentry to the neigh- bourhood, and it will be seen that some of the " cutest of the cute "visited the premises indicated. About half-past one o'clock three or few apparently respectable and moder- ately well-to-do young men entered the shop and asked to be served with dinner. They talked and chatted in a fami- liar manner about the positions they would occupy at the the table, and in doing so—as has since been unfortunately I discovered—they came unnecessarily near the kind and un- suspecting Mrs. Johnson. One of the men suddenly made I an excuse for leaving the shop "for a few moments," and ' his companions shortly afterwards followed him. The re- sult was that almost directly afterwards it was discovered by Mrs. Johnson that her visitors and pretending customers bad dexterously relieved her pocket of a.purse, which con- tained over £3 in cash. We regret to have to announce that the gang of scoundrels escaped with their booty, and having become lost In the crowd, little hope of their capture Is held.

APPRNHENDRD oN LEAVING PE/SO:7,—A young man named Walter Devan, of Earlestown, was charged, at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Thursday, with stealing a shirt, value 7s. from an entry in Water-street, on January 19th, the property of Joseph Powell. Prisoner only came out of Manchestsr Gaol on Wednesday. fie was fines £l, or 14 days.

-FOOTBALL CONTEST AT ASHTON.—On reference to OUT advertising columns, it will be seen that the annual sports in connection with the Ashton Reereation Society will be held on Whit-Monday. One of the features will be a foot- ball contest for teams of seven players. The following will play for the Earlestowe club :—G. Whalley (captain), G. Clough, R. Green, J. Green, J. W. Sims, T. Sid&ley, and W. Rich.

SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT TEE RAcEs.—On Wednesday afternoon Mrs. Connolly, residing near the Oak Tree Inn, Newton, met with a serious accident in Market-street, Ear- lestown. About half-past four o'clock she was leaving the shop of Mr. T. Molyneux, provision dealer, and as she was crossing the street, at that moment crowded with vehicles and people returning from the races, when she was knocked down by one of the numerous traps. One of the wheels passed over her, and she was seriously injured and bruised. She was taken to a shop in the vicinity, and afterwards re- moved to the surgery of Dr. Valentine, Oxford-street, where she was attended to. CRUELTY AT NEWTON Famt.—Brian Conroy, or Con- way, a cattle dealer residing at St. Helens, was summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions. on Saturday, for cruelty to a horse by working it in an unfit state, at Newton Cattle Fair, on the 17th ult.—The defendant did not aopear.—From the evidence of two inspectors of the Royal Society for the Pre- vention of Cruelty to Animals it appeared that on the date named the defendant was in charge of a bay gelding. He was proceeding along High-street, Newton, and the horse seemed extremely lame. On being spoken to the defendant said it bad been lame for a month. The horse was totally unfit for any kind of work.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s and costs.

THE Flo=Am.—During the present week—Race week—no attempt at a uniform holiday for the workmen in the district, has been made by the employers. It may be stated, however, that the Viaduct works, belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Company, were kept going on Tuesday and Wednesday, though many of the handi asked off for the afternoons of Tuesday and Wed- nesday ; the men employed by the Sankey Sugar C, mpar.y were kept at work on both days; the Vulcan ironfoundry was stopped for the 2 full days ; Messrs. Vicars stopped on Tuesday afternoon and all day on Wednesday, and Messrs. Slee and Co. stopped on both afternoons only. Very few, if any, of the shops or places of business were closed on either day.

-GOOD TionmAnY.—The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held on Mon- day night. Brother James McDonald, W.C.T., presided, and there was a good attendance. Brother John Warburton L.D, read a circularefrom the G.W.C.T. upon matters affec- ting the Order, aud Brother John Taylor, W.C., one of the lodge representatives at the District Lodge reported thereon. Brother George Clarke's report on the tea party and finan- cial arrangements in connection with the District Lodge session at Earlestown en Saturday last was of a satisfactory character and was unanimously adopted. Brother James Flaherty, formerly of Earlestown, who was on a visit from Manchester, gave an interesting address at the conclusion of the lodge business.

THE WZGAN AND DISTRICT FOOTBALL ASSOCIATION.— The annual fleeting of this association was held at the Railway Hotel, Wigan, last week, when representatives from the following among other clubs were present, viz. : Ashton Recreation, Earlestown, Varlestown Wanderers, Haydock Association, Haydock St. James's, Haydock C. B. and F., Golborne. Mr. D. B. Marsh (Ashton) was voted to the chair. Mr. Bennett, Westhoughton, was el.cted hon. treasurer, and Mr. G- H. Hunt, Elder-terrace. Haydock, sec- retarv. The following gentlemen were elected to serve on the Executive Committee, viz., Mr. R. Green (Westhough- ton F.C.), Mr. F: J. Baldwin (Wigtn), Mr. P. Riinford (Haydock C. B. and F.), Mr. T. Harrison (Haydock St. James's), Mr. J. H. Mi4dlehurst (Ashton), Mr. Lomax (Ad- lington), Mr. W. Dootson (Hindley), Mr. J. Robinson (Park. lane), Mr. W. Tanstall (Haydock Association), Mr. John Jones (Springs Branch Rovers), Mr. W. Limond (Fades- town Wanderers), Mr. J. Sankey (Golborne), Mr. P. Hastie (Earlestown).

PRESENTATION TO A SUNDAY SCHOLAR.—An interest- ing incident was witnessed in the Brunswick Wesleyan sunday School, Cross-lane. Earlestown, on Sunday after- noon, when Mr. Williatn Gore, better known as William Gore Kelly, of Queen-street, one of the scholars in the first class, was presented with a handsomely-bound copy of the Bible, on leaving the school to join the Royal Navy. The Bible bore the following inecriptien :—" Presented to Wm. Gore by the officers and teachers of the Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School. Elarlestown, on the occasion of his joining her Mejesty's Navy. John Barr and Thomas Clare super- intendents, Samuel Barrett secretary ; Earleetown, May 30th, 1886." The presented was made by Mr. John Barr (superintendent), who tastefully alluded to the circum- stances under which the recipient was leaving them, and expressed a hope it would help him to keep in the right course of life, and would he a light to his feet and a lamp to his path. Master Gore expressed his thanks for their kind gift. CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL• TREAT.—TEe an- nual treat to the scholars attending the Congregational Sunday School, Crow-lane, was held on Wednesday after- noon. The scholars to the number of 350 met at the schoolroom about two o'clock, and were formed in proces- sional order. Among those present were the Rev. James Allatt, pastor, Mr. B. B. Glover (superintendent), and the teachers and officers. The procession was headed by a handsome new banner, purchased for the Sunday school from Messre. Hitchen and Squire, Liverpool. They marchod along Crow-lane, and subsequently entered into the field of the Earlestown Football Club, on the Mesnes, and which had been kindly lent for the occasion. Here the scholars spent the afternoon in various games' including races for small prizes, and a football match. Two large paper balloons had been brought into the field, but it was impos- sible to get them afloat owing to the very strong wind which prevailed. During the afternoon the scholars -were served with buns and milk. LIEUDENT ROBBERY OR A GANDER.—Before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and W. F. Gooch, at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Richard Martin, a middle-aged man, was charged with stealing a gander. value 20s, the property of John Bridge, Old Hey Farm, Wargrave. —Superintendent Weir stated that on the previous Thurs- day morning about nine o'clock Mr. Bridge saw his gander safe on the farm. A little later the prisoner was seen by Edmued Jordan, a pointsman on the railway, with a sack on his shoulders, near the railway. He saw he was carrying something in the sack, and he communicated with a plate- layer named Alexander Ward, who followed the prisoner and brought him back. He had the gander in the sack, and its head was Cut off. The prosecutor Bridge had missed the gander, and was coming down the road when he met the man Ward with the prisoner. The prisoner said he would give 105 if he (Bridge) would let him go-away, but prosecu- tor declined to do so. A knife covered with blood and small feathers wee afterwards found in prisoner's possession.—Evi- dence was given by the prosecutor, Edmund Jordan, and Samuel Ward, the latter stating that he saw the prisoner running from the back of Mr.. Bridge's farm with the gander in his hands—P.C. McMullen said he apprehended the prisoner, who made no repiy. He found on prisoner a pocket knife covered with blood and small feathers. He asked prisoner if it was his knife, and he replied, " Yes ; that's the knife I killed it with."—The prisoner was sent to prison for six weeks with hard labour. TREAT TO THE VITRIOL•SQUARH CHILDREN. The annual treat, provided by the Sankey Sugar Company, to the children of the tenants of Vitriol-square, and the scho- lars attending the Vitriol-square Day and Sunday schools, took place on Tuesday afternoon. Unfortunately the wea- ther was very wet, and considerably interfered with the afternoon's pleasure. The children, nambering about 200, met at the schoolroom about half-past two, and the pro- cession was postponed owing to the rain. They amused themselves in various games until about four o'clock, when they partook of a substantial tea. The arrangements were carried out by Mr. Wm. Thompson, senior, Mr. Herbert Thompson, Captain Thompson, Messrs. T. Haselden, T. Kenny, T. Millard, C. Millard, J. Millard, Mrs ;ate, Mrs Haselden, the itEsses Thompson, Platt, Kenyon, Wrigley, Underwood, ecc. The children were subsequently formed in procession, and headed by the Edge Green Brass Band, marched throtteh Vitriol-square and on to Sankey Hill, where Captain Thompson spoke a few encouraging words to them, giving them a hearty welcome, and expressed his sorrow that owing to the rain they were unable to enjoy themselves in the field. On returning to the school they again indulged in games, and as the weather cleared a little the girls-played in the volunteer drill yard, and the boys in the square. At the close the children gave hearty cheers for the Sankey Sugar Company. ANTI- VA.CCZNATORs SUMMONED. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and W. F. Gooch, William Noble, of Nelson- street, Earlestown was summoned for failing to have his child vaccinated within the time specified by the Vaccine- I tion Acts. Mr. A. Cooper, vaccination officer, conducted I the proseoution.—Defendant said he had not been given a• reasonable time to have his child vaccinated since Mr. Cooper gave him notice about it. When he was served with the notice he had the children down with fever, and he had bad them down with chicken-pox since.—Mr. Cooper said he had called at defendant's house, but was unable to see anybody.—The Bench made an order for the child to be vaccinated within three weeks.—John Mottrarn, of EArles- town, was summoned for a similar offence—Mrs. Mottram said they bad one child vaccinated, and it was bad for eight months afterwards. Her daughter was either bleeding or covered with black scabs from the head to the waist.—ThO Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Buckton): That was some other c'uild ; we must talk about this one.—Mrs. Mottram : Yes, but that is the reason why we have not had this one vac- cinated. She was in a terrible state, and that is why we have not had it done—The Chairman: The child must be vaccinated within three weeks.—Robert Taylor, of Earles- town, was summoned for a similar offence. The defend- ant's wife appeared in answer to the summons.—Mr. Cooper stated that he called at TaylOr's house on the previous Mon- day, and Mrs. Taylor said she did not believe in vaccina- tion. He called again on the Tuesday, and Mr. Taylor said he would not have it done.—The Chairman : What reason have you for not having it done? Mrs. Taylor: A nephew of mine lost his child through vaccination.—The Bench made an order tor the child to be vaccinated within three weeks, •

DIEGRACEFITL Col/DTJOT AT NEWTON' COMIC:M.—At he Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and W, F. Gooch, James Virater- worth. a middle-aged man residing at Newton Common, was summoned for using threatening language to Samuel Bro Was a neighbour, on the Saturday night previous.—Mr. Browns, of Warrington, who appeared for the complainant. stated that the defendant and complainant were both miners, and lived in adjoining houses. On the night in question com- plainant and his wife were sitting in the house with a Mt. and Mrs. Thomas, when they heard a disturbance in defen- dant's house. The defendant afterwards knocked at tbe front door of complainant's house, and said to complainant, "It's thee I want." The defendant, who bad nothing on but his shirt, behaved in an improper manner, and used threatw ing language to tho complainant.—Evidence to this effect was given, and the Bench bound defendant aver to keep the pace for six months.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

Mr. Joseph Leigh has been chosen Liimral candidate lOC Stockport. The second candidate is not yet selected. The tenants on the Drake of Bedford's Devon, Corti'. wall, and Dorset estates have received 15 per cent. rent reduction. On Monday, at Leigh, Wm. Barton, butcher, was oollinsit7 tEI to two months' hard laboue for exposing putrid meat Of sale in the Market-place. Mr. C. H. Hopwood, Q.C. formerly one of the Liberal members for Stockport„ has intimated that he does not again intend to contest the borough. Tee Richmond Vestry on Thursday night decided to SO' cept the offer of the Duke of Baccleuch to sell to the vestri his Richmond estate for £30,900. At Taunton, on Saturday, Jane Nicholls, a young dotuns; tic servant from Battersea, was sentenced to twentV Years penal servitude for drowning her baby. A fire on Saturday night in Berlin, completely destrolea several industrial establishments, and damage was done t° the extent of £200.000. A woman was burnt to death. Mrs. Shine, a large landed proprietor in KilkennY, sold her Galway property to the tenants at prices varYine from 15 to 10 years' purchase, forgiving all arrears of rent- The new sewerage works at Sheffield, which have bee° constructed at a cost of £150,000, were formally opened 0° Wednesday by the mayor of that town. A number of brewers and others met on Tuesday, at the Cannon-street Hotel. London, and adopted a resolution de. Oaring that the Pure Beer Bill should be opposea. „ Fields of ice, hundreds of miles in extent and contain many hundreds of icebergs, are floating about off the Cana,: dian coast, making a direction right in the track of AVOW' steamers. About 70 persons hays been drowned by the wreck, °,ll. Sunday, of the Australian Steam Navigation Comeani,„S steamer Sytmoon, off dreen Cape, while on a voyage fro"' Melbourne to Sydney. At a meeting of the Liverpool Town Council, on Wednes- nt, day, an aminated discassicn arose .on the motion to gr,ar, £12,000 to the Mayor to defray the cost of the Royal vie"' The grant was finally agreed to. Dublin, with a garrison of nearly 4,000 men in its eig te ht barracks, is to have an additional barrack built en a I close to the Royal Irish Constabulery DepotePlalsnix at an estimated cost of .£112,000. At Folkestone, on Monday, a gentleman, his wife, end little boy—named Boscoe—went for a sail, when the boat capsized, and the lady and boy were drowged. Mr. Bost° was rescued in an exhausted condition. ' According to present arrangements thl Queen t will return to Windsor Castle from Balmoral on the 20th least. Øer Majesty's sojourn in the Highlands may, however, be cur' tailed by the exigencies of public affairs. THE ICIRKHAM MURDER.—The constable Bligh continues eel make good progress. He is still watched day and nigh!' When fit he will be removed to Preston Gaol. Bligh 0 visited by the vicar of Weston. He remains silent to the tragedy. Professor Sheldon read a paper before the Farmers' Alt ance on the " Butterine Question." In the discussion whic° followed the opinion was expressed that some legislation was required to protect the public from fraud and farmeo from an unfair competition. The annual show in connection with the Bath and West of England Agricultural Society was opened at Bristol on Wednesday. The exhibition is described as a good one, considering the depressed condition of agriculture and the state of the weather recently. Sixteen young lads drifted into Dublin Bay from Blach- rock on Sunday night on four rafts on which they had bee° amusing themselves. Coastguardsmen and fishermen went out in search of them, and by one o'clock on Mondai morning all the children had been rescued. Mr. Labouchere, M.P., writing to congratulate the Pontve pridd Liberals upon forming a Junior Liberal Associatioo. says he trusts the club will be a success in these days whe° the Tories are organising Primrose Leagues and getting blank cheques from Dukss for the purpose of cerruption. A WINDFALL OF £3o.ooo.—Three persons in humble li• fe at Fdenderry, King's County, have just succeeded i° establishing their claim to about £30,000, left by a cousin, f Robert Higgins, who emigrated to America in the famine . period, and died at Albany, State of New York,. in January', 1885. MILL FIRE AT DARWEN. A fire occurred early Or,' Thursday morning at India Mill, one of the largest Oa , finest twinning concerns in Darwen. lhe damage, which - ; chiefly caused by water, will arneunt to several thousand pounds. It will be some weeks before the mill' can be re' ' started. About 300 hands are thrown out. DESTRUCTIVE FIRRS.—The Forest-road Lace Mills, Net' tingham, were on Wednesday destroyed by fire, causing damage to the extent of £B,OOO, and throwing many Per sons out of employment. The old church of Shustoke.lo Warwickshire, has been almost completely destroyed bi lightning. Other fires of a more or less destructive nature, caused by lightning or otherwise, arc reported. OUTRAGE IN IRELAND—Five much cows, the pronerti of Patrick Kerin, a farmer, have been mutilated at Dre" mouin. Their ears and tails were cut off, and two bad their legs broken. Punctured wounds from which the blood flowed were also visible on the hides of the beasts. Tv/0 causes are assigned—one that Kerin was suspected of having, I Paid his rent, and the other that he put cattle on boycotted I land. There is no clue to the offenders. SEIZURE OF Arms IN IRELAND.—It is reported that for some time rifles and t words have been arriving here cone signed to various parts of Ulster, but they were detained by the police until further information regarding them had been received. On Sunday morning' a coneignment for firm at Armagh arrived by the Fleetwood steamer, this consisting of about a dozen rifles, together with bayonete and it was detained by the Custom House authorities.

THE QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY.—The Queen's birthday was celebrated officially in London on Saturday by the ceremonf of trooping the colours of the Household Regiments, on the Horse Guards Parade, St. James's Park. The day being fitie, there was a large and brilliant gathering on the Parade grounds, while the Park and Mibll were filled with thousands of spectators. The Prince slid Princess of Wales wore present, his Royal Highness 10 uniform.

DESTRUCTIVB Frnms.—About two o'clock on Tueeds3r morning a fire broke out on the premises of Mr. T. Enver, ; a miller, Lciicester. Th.e rocf soon fell in. and the structure ' was completely gutt.d. All tbe valual,le plant and machine were destroyed. A fire occurred on Monday night at a spitv !ling mill known as Whittaker's Old Mill, Luzley Broolro Oldham. The flames got a thorough bold of the building, which was completely .././tt,d, and all the machinery des' troyed. The damage will amount to about £25,000. SEIIOI7B ACCIDENT TO A POLICE.IIAN.-011 Moridai night, P.C. John Macdonald, a member of the St. Heleng division of Lancashire County Constabulary, who nad been away on fourteen days' leave of absence, was returning te his station at Rainford, and took the nearest route by the Rainford branch of the London sod North-Western Railwai• On nearing Moss Bank he was knocked down by an al); proacbing engine and run over,his right foot and right haV being badly crushed. As soon as possible Macdonald W3e removed to the Moss Bank Hotel, and on Tuesday morning taken to the Providence Hospital, where he is being attended by Dra.Twvford and Jamison.

TUB ROCK FERRY MURDER.—When Captain Price governor of Knutsford gaol, received the commutation of the sentence of death passed upon Robert Travis, hotel' keeper, he, in company with the chaplain, the Rev. W; Truss, went at once to the condemned man's cell and cernmunicated the intelligence. Travis,. whose whole cow' cern has been for his family, expressed himself delighted, but declared himself not guilty of the crime, which he hto eturdfly done ever since ha stood in the dock, when bin parting words were a declaration of innocence. Captain Price expects to receive an older for the convict's remova! to Stafford gaol in about a month, and from thence he vii 4 be consigbed to a convict establishment to work out hiS terrible sentence of life imprisonment.

• A NEW COLLIERY Al PARE.—A dinner to eelebrate the fine.ing of co dat the new Little Dolph Mine, at the ' Ash-tons Green CoHieries of MeFers. Dromilow, Foster, and Co., was held at the Royal Raven Hotel, on Friday evening' The collieries, which are situate at Parr, were taken over 139 the company named about three years ago, and sines then no expense, notwithstanding the depression in the coal trade, has been spared to extend their operations, and W provide employment for the numerous workpeople in the neighbourhood. The Rushy Park Mine was reached five weeks ago, and the Little Delph Mine on Tuesday week, 313_ engineering feat which for the time is unparalleled in t°' district. The Little Delpti seam it is claimed is equal to the Wigan Arley, and great expectations are formed as to the results of the explorations. The company os Friday nigh_,%l which included all those who had been actively engage' with Mr. Piggott, assembled at the Raven Hotel shortli after half-past six o'clock, and sat down to a splendid re; past. The viands were excellent in quality, well conkef: and equally well served. Mr. Thomas Pennington, manager of the collieries, presided, and he was supported Mr. Piggott, Mr. J. T. Elliott (cishier), Mr. E. F. (surveyor), Mr. J. Seddon (mechanical engineer), Mr. Winsard (Wigan), and Messrs. J. Maddeson, J. Woods, .1; Lawrenson, J. Rotherham, dm. The usual loyal toasts Neel, honoured, after which the Chairman proposed " Success h 1; Messrs. Bromilow, Foster, and Company,* and spoke of 11 operations carried out by Mr. Piggott, who suffeuars responded, The Town and Trade of St. Helens " gives by Mr. Winnard, and responded to by Mr. E. Seddon; "The Company's Officials," proposed by Mr. A. PenningtO and responded to by Mr. J. Seddon ; and several other toast: were duly honoured. The harmony of the evening was Wu trihuted to by Miss and Mager liarfout, and Mears, Elliott, Wooda, and Foster.

div.head: WIT AND HUMOUR.
div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

Matter of form—The wearing of corsets. • When a Chicago man does a good deed, the people erect a moehment to his honour. There are no monuments in Chicago. LESSON IN ManerEns.--gmall boy: "Ma, pass the bread." Mother, sternly: "If what my son ?" Small boy, smartly: "If you can reach it.'' A Way THBY HAYB TICE ARMY.—Mistrees: "Jane, what is the matter with your hair ?" Servant: "It's the Cavalry regiment, ma'am ; they all wanted a lock of My hair before they left 1" A class in natural history being asked the difference between a dog and a tree, the head boy answered, "A tree is covered wite bark, while a dog seems to be lined with it." Solicitor, to new clerk: "You don't seem to keep pace with my dictation. Why don't you write short-hand? You told me you knew short-band." Clerk: "So I do; but it takes me longer than ordinary writing." A lady, looking at some apartments, inquired of the land- lord, "How about the stairway ?" " Oh, it excellent, madam !" he answered. "When you are going up, it is so easy that you imagine that you are descending" " What ! Women overworked? Fudge! Think of the men!" "Ah, but you know the old saying, Woman's work is never done !' " " I know it; aqd that's the reason she oughtn t to complain; for a man has to do his work or lose his job !" CONJUGAL AFFECTION.—Husband : "And so, doctor, von think my wife will get well y Doctor: "I am sure of it, if you can persuade her to take this medicine." Husband-: "Doctor, take it she shall, if I have to break every bone in her body !" Young actor: "Have you been down to see me act lately, old boy ?" Friend: "No; too poor." Young actor: "Non- sense! Why, you spend money enough on cigars in a week to buy a doz-n tickets!" Friend: "Oh, I don't mean I'm too poor! You're too poor !" JUST ONE SIDE OF THE TOPIC.—" At what time did you get home from the club last night, Jack ?" "At three in the morning." "Awakening your wife, no doubt ?" "Yes, Tom. That's my usual luck, you know." "What did you say ?" "I didn't say anything. There wasn't anything left to say after she had finished !" Jones, a Manchester nouveau riche, and his son, intent on foreign travel, were buying a guide to Austria at a book- seller's. To aesure himself of its accuracy, Jones junior tried to find Moscow. Jones senior assisted him in this hopeless task. At the end of five minutes Jones junior, in despair, was About to throw the book aside as worthless, when his father was suddenly inspired. "No wonder you can't find it," he exclaimed—" you forget that Moscow was burned !" The accomplished wife—now dead—of General Hooker, when she was the admired Miss Groesbeck of Cincinnati, was once at an evening party when a fashionable young dandy was asked if he would like to be presented to her. "Oh, yes," said he languidly—" trot her out!" The lady overheard the remark; and, when he was presented, she 'adjusted her eye-glasses deliberately, and slowly scanned his clothing from trot to collar. The survey finished, ehe waved her hind and said carelessly," Trot him back !" LEGAL FOG.—It was a case in the United States District Court at Albany some little time back.- A patent-right suit was brought before Judge Nelson. air. William H. Seward ' was counsel on one side. In summing up he occupied a whole day. The counsel on the other side Made a long speech, and the judge charged the jury. After the jury had been absent about two hours, they came into court, and the foreman said, "Your honour, the jury would like to ask a question." "You can proceed." "Well, Your honour, we ' should like to know what this suit is about." A gentleman at a recent matinee at a theatre in the Strand was seated behind a lady wearing one of the new fashion- able hats. "Excuse me, madam; but if you do not remove your hat, I shall not be able to see anything." The lady ignored him. "Excuse me, madam; but, if you do not remove your hat, something unpleasant will happen." The lady ignored him again. The gentleman put on his own hat Loud cries of "Take off that hat! Take off that hat !" arose from the audience behind. The lady thought the c: ies referred to her hat, and removed it. "Thank you, madam !" STRANGE PRESORIPTION.—A Scotch lad was 0111 one Occa- sion accused of stealing some articles from a doctor's shop. The judge was much struck with his respectable appearance, and asked him why he was guilty of such a coutemptible act. "Weel, ye see," replied the prisoner, "I had a bit pain in my side, and thy neither tauld me tae gang tae the doctor's and tak' something-" "Oh, yes!" said the judge. "But surely she didn't tell you to go and take an eight-day clock?" The prisoner was evidently nonplused, but it was only for a moment. Turning to the judge, a bright smile of humour stealing over his countenance, he replied quietly, "There's an auld proverb that says, Time an' the doctor cure a' diseases,' an' sae I thocht"—but the remainder of the reply was lost in the laughter of the court. Soule I—A few years ago, when a Scottish Parliamentary candidate was canvassing his constituency, he called at the house of an aged couple. Finding the old woman alone, he entered into conversation with her, and asked her to use her influence in getting her husband to vote for him. While they were conversing, the would-be M.P. noticed a kitten amusing itself on the floor, and, taking it up, praised its beauty, and offered her five pounds for it. The bargain was struck; and, on leaving, he again expressed the hope that she would secure her hueband's vote for him. "Weel, sir," answered the woman, "as I said afore, John's a man o' his am n mind, an' just does what stricks his am n noddle; but, at ony rate, sir, you've gotten a rale cheap kitten, for yer op- ponent was in nae farer gene than yesterday, an' gae me ten pounds for its brither." It is impossible not to be greatly amused at some of the typographical errors of the day—it seems as if nothing quite so grotesque could have happened before; but reference to newspaper-files of past generations shows that the humours of types are not restrained by time. The late Dr. Francis tells an anecdote bearing on the subject. John Lang was the editor of the old New _York Gazette when scholastic discussions on the question of the beginning of the present century were not uncommon. The Rev. Dr. Cunze, very learned and pious, addressed, after much in- vestigation, a communication on the subject to the editor. Be referred to the Gregorian style and Pope Gregory, which Use printers made "Tom Gregory." The reverend doctor, deeply distressed, demanded an editorial correction that "Tom Gregory" meant "Pope Gregory X.III." The Gazette accordingly requested its readers to understand for "Tom Gregory,' in a previous issue, "Pope Tom Gregory XIII." Another effort was made to eat the matter right, and the result was that mention was made of "Tom Gregory the Pope !" The erudite clergyman, in utter despair, requested the editor to try nothing more in the way of correction, as he feared that he should lose all the reputation acquired by years of devotion to the subject at isles. Keens BY ThigeßAPll.—" Weel, did ye get my letters, Jeannie ?" asked Jock Tamson of his buxom sweetheart, to whom he had returned after a six months' absence. "&y, an' yer kisses too, Jock," said Jeannie slily. "Oh, the crosses !" laughed Jock. "They werena sae sweet kisses as thee anes, I warrant !"—and he bestowed a hearty smack on the upturned face. "Weel, I'm no sae sure, though they've a queer-like taste when they come by telegraph," said Jeannie. "By telegraph!" echoed Jock, in an amazed way. "Ay," returned Jeannie. "Ye see, I never kent what the crosses at the fit o' yer letters were for, till ae dae I speired at Jess Myers, an' she tell't me they were a receipt for twenty kisses ye had sent to me by telegraph, an' that they wid be lyin' waitin' me at the Post-office."
