VEGETARIANISM IN THE LIVERPOOL EX EtIBI [ION.

Sir,—ln inviting attention to the Vegetarian Society's Work at the Liverpool Exhibition, perhaps I may be per- mitted to mention that the dininE room is not opened as a profit-making concern, but is educational in its purposes; and it is in the interests of the general public that we desire te make it widely known. Our aim is to demonstrate the pleasantness, variety, wholesomenees, economy, dec., of the food products of the 'vegetable kingdem, miny of which might, ith advantage, be more generally used than they are at present. There are not wanting evidences that were the principles of vege- tarianism more widely known and followed—especially by the wage-earning classes—the benefits following thereon would be not merely of an individual or even sectional character. but by their gradual extension and the consequent improvement in home agriculture, combined with a leessned expenditure in bringing food from abroad, there would be less poverty, greater prosperity, and a higher degree of peace and contentment throughout the entire nation.—Yours faithfully, JOSEPH KNIGHT, Secretary.

div.head: MUSIC IN THE PARK.
div.p: MUSIC IN THE PARK.

Sir,—Having seen a notice posted at our works to the effect tnat there would be a " Bend in the Park this even- ing at 745," and being a lover of music, I thought I would indulge in the pleasure afforded by the sweet harmonies after a hard day's work. I went full of glee and expect- ancy to the musical promenade, when the band struck up with a lively march, enough to mako the most downcast heart leap with joy. I was filled with the thrill and en- ergy which a martial march alone can give, until I heard the lively strains of a romping polka, a step-a-leng-pull-me- round schwtische, or the seductive powers of the most charming of dances, the waltz. When I heard the band playing dance music, I expected to sea some dancing, but no ; on looking round I percelved that " expectation " was there in plenty. but that was what had to be, for 'realisa- tion " was st, ictly prohibited, I was told, on making in- quiry. And why ? I asked. " Oh, lam sore I cannot tell you," was the reply. Here were scores of young people listening to the band, suffering the torture which d.lncers alone can feel when they hear the soul-thrilling mu4c which draws them round as if by magic. You can listen, but to respond is strictly prohibited. Pat temptation within reach, and the wily cues will accept of it; keep temptation away ("lead us not into temp- tation"), and we are not influenced to partake of it. What I propose to the Music Committee (who I am sure deserve our most cordial support and thanks for their energy) is, to advise the conductors of the obliging bands not to include dance music their programmes, but treat us to good classi- cal selections; or to bring their influence to bear upon the Park Committee to allow dancing, which I am sure would be gladly apprrciated by at least eighty out of every hundred who patronise the band with their presence and purse. Thanking you for publishing the above, am, your' very truly, A NOVICE. Warrington, June 2nd, 1886.

Allow me now, Sir, to quote from the pamphlet referred to. In the Crown Colony of Hong Kong, two Chinese women were, in October, 1877, killed by falling from the roof of a house over which they were endeavouring to escape from the police employed to carry out the Contagious Dis- eases Acts of the colony. The coroner's jury passed a severe censure on the system under which this happened; and the Governor of Ilong Kone, Sir J. Pope Hennessy, wrote to Lord Carnarvon, who was then Co!onial Srcretary, informing him of what bad taken place. In this letter Governor Hennessy remarks—" I have taken the responsi- bility of putting a stop to the appropriation of Government money for the pay of informers, who might induce Chinese women to prostitute themselves, and thus bring them under the penal clauses of the C4ntagious Diseases Acts. I had no idea that the secret service fund was used for this loath- some purpose." It would be impossible to go further into this matter. _

The more the working classes know of the corruption that prevailed throughout the whole of the Government departments, and the more they will honour and revere the memory of departed Radicals, and be prepared to help the Radicals of to-day. The spending of Secret Service Money is but one of maav ways in which the people are mis- governed by a proud and arrogant class. A Minister, how- ever capable he may be, can only accomplish what the people have decided upon. Influence of a kind little dreamt of by the masses is brought to bear upon him, until, weary with the struggle, he determines to swim with the stream. We have seen, since the Irish que,titni became a burning one, bow Mr. Gladstone has, time after time, been deserted by men who cannot possibly be made to see that the interest of the wholcepeople must stand before that of Individuals. This has been done so often that at length be has in his recent manifesto told us bluntly that it is class interest and this oniy that stands ha the way of reform. With the spending of the people's money wk. must not lose sight of the " placcmen." These and the salaries they are kind enough to pocket for their services may be noticed at some future time. CLIFFORD DIX. June 2nd, 1886.

div.head: RESISTANCE THE PRICE OF VICTORY.
div.p: RESISTANCE THE PRICE OF VICTORY.

Sir,—l: is sometimes said that anti•vaccinators damage a good case by the use of intemperate language, but it is only fair to remember that great injustice in any civlized com- munity will always produce strong feelings of iedignation and remonstrance. When the great American reformer, William Lleyd Garrison, the leader of the antislavery agitation was accused of using harsh language towards the northero upholders and abettors of chattel elavery such as is now sometimes used against the defenders of vaccine tyranny, he replied :—" I will be as harsh as truth, I will be as uncompromising as justice, I will not equivecate, I wilt not retreat, and I will be heard." We know the result, and if those who are carrying on the aqitation against cone- pulsery vaccination (an evil of scarcely less magnitude then that against which the Garrisonian party waged righteous warfare in Americt) will be equally faithful and pers'stent a few years at most will witness its entire overthrow. Forty years ago, the cry of those earnest reformers who were trying to give untaxed bread to the poor was that thousinds of women and children were starving for want of that sostenence which the Corn Law kept out of the coun- try. Our cry, which is neither less piteous nor less true, Is that thousands of children born of healthy parentage are suffering aud dying through the indiction of this system of universal State laq)od poisoning, and Rechele are weeping all over the land for their childrea which are not. All true friends should then resolve, irrespective of sect (Y- party (for no political party holds a monopoly of sympathy for the suffering victims of cruelty and injustice), to use all legitimate means by public meetings. discussions. and writing to the press, and particularly by preesiug this facts upon candidates and members of Parliament of exposing this mischievous delusion, so that Parliament can have no rest until the despotic Vaccination Laws are repealed. The decisive and overwhelming rejection of the National Vac- cination Law in Switzerland has illustrated what a free people can do when their liberties are assailed —Yours Lab fully, WILLIAM TEBB, F.R.Ci.S. National Liberal Club, Charing Cross, London, May 29..1888.

SECRET SERVICE MONEY. Sir,—lt is possible some good may come of the recent dis- cussion in the House on Secret Service Money. One bV eine these remnants of a system which enabled monarch's to rule Parliament, and by these means keep the people in subjection are being brought to light. It is not only royalty. bet the whole of our Parliamentaay system, which is brought under the strong light of public opinion. Can anyone say why £50,000 should be yearly spent in Secret Service? Or why the estimates should include .S3O 000 out of this sum, voted in a careless and ignorant Inner? Ignorance there must be, for here we have Mr. Ciladstone, the foremost of our financial statesmen, assert- ing that he knows nothing whatever of the matter. Since 1837 all parties in the State have had the control of the Public purse, and have, there is no doubt, made good use of it, and now, when Mr Rylands makes an attempt to reduce it by the sum of £5.000, both parties, Liberals and Tories, join their forces to defeat it, and in this they are successful, and will be, so long as we send men to Parliament whose Only object in life is self. It cannot be said that all the Ministers are in ignorance as to bow Secret Service Money is spent. A short time ago a pamphlet was issued lay the National Association for the repeal of he Ciotagious Diseases Acts, with an introduc- tion by the Right Hon. James Stansfield, M.P., containing statements which should at once have brought down the Whole fabric about the ears of its supporters. It is not enough to say we have confidence in Mr. Gladstone or any Other of the high-minded gentlemen who kindly sacrifice themselves for their country's good. They are, to a lage extent, instruments in the hands of the permanent officiate, and cannot look after details, and it is only when the official veil is lifted that we get a glimpse of what isigoing cc.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTEit
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTEit
LONDON, THURSDAY.

The great division on which depends the fate of the Ministry, and, it may be, the welfare of the country for six years to come, is still deferred. A fortnight ago Tuesday last was named as the day. At the beginning of thiFweek Thursday was fixed upon. Then Friday was named, and at the present moment there is every prospect of its going over to next week. Whenever it comes it will be the biggest division that has ever taken place in the House of Commons. That assembly is now numerically larger than it has been when, on any former occasion, challenged to a declaration of opinion. The Conservatives count upon bringing every one of their men into the lobby save Mr. Macarteny, who is on a sick bed. The Irishmen may be depended upon for their 86 votes. The Liberals will be sharply whipped up, and the combined factions of Whigs and Radicals will, be looked after by Lord liartington and Mr. Chamberlain.

As to the result it is more than usually difficult , to forecast. All kind of speculations are current, . giving the Opposition majority at from ten to ' to thirty-five. What is notable in the matter.is that all the computations agree in giving the ma- jority against the Government. It may be larger or it may be smaller; but it is agreed that it will come to pass. There are sr me who, without aging into particulars of figures, express a vague hope that at the last moment some of the declared dissi- dents will "come over and help us." It would be rash to denounce this opinion as illusory. The course of events has been so varying that anything may be expected. Writing last week I had to record a state of things which seemed to point to the cer- tainty of the second reading being carried. Then came the meeting of the Chamberfainites on Mon- day, and the whole aspect of affairs was changed. It may change again within the next forty-eight hours, though at present I see no prospect of its doing so. There is. I fear, little doubt that we are on the eve of a dissolution, an event to be regretted from many points of view. Coming in the height of the sea- son, it will be a bad thing for trade already groan- ing under continued depression. Arriving just now it finds the Liberal party in a state of disunion, and, not the least deplorable consideration, it forces the General Election before the new register is com- pleted. It is the gravest charge against Mr. Cham- berlain and his friends that. all -these calamities might have been avoided had they displayed a little patience and consideration. Mr. Gladstone, respect- ing their conscientious scruples, made it very easy for them to vote for the second reading of the pre- sent bill upon the understanding that they were not doing more than approving the principle of Home Rule, leaving the details of a measure em- bodyinr, it to be discussed at leisure in the autumn. Everybody knows that we must have a dissolution before a Home Rule Bill is added to the statute book. Most people agree that it would not be well , long to delay the appeal to the country. But there is immense virtue in six months delay, and it will not be forgotten against Mr. Chamberlain that ho is responsible for refusing this concession. The General Election, whetner it comes early in July or early in January, will be fought under pecu- liar circumstances. We shall in many constituen- cies have Liberals standing against Liberals, and Conservatives quietly walking in to secure the seat. From the general point of view the great bulk of the party remaining faithful to Mr. Gladstone will fight under exceptionally difficult circumstances. The Liberal party could very well spare the Whig Dukes and Marquises who have seceded. But the fact is that these gentlemen in times past have liberally contributed the sinews of war at election contests. They have not only gone, but they have taken their money bags with them, and mean to use their contents in despite of Mr. Gladstone and the popular will. Mr. Gladstone himself, I believe, regards this circumstance with a light heart. He has an illimitable faith in the people, and expresses it to the effect that when the fact becomes known that the Liberal party is labouring under disadvan- tages owing to lack of money abundantly supplied by the seceders, there will be a movement among the people that will speedily set the balance right. The people least troubled in these stirring times are the Irish members. They are enthusiastic in their loyalty to Mr. Gladstone, and may be counted upon to do all they can at the coming election to estab- lish his power. But, save for personal reasons, they are wholly indifferent to the issue. They know that the concession of Home Rule is inevitable, and will be made within the next two years, whatever party is in power. They would rather obtain it through Mr. Gladstone, having fuller hope in his sympathy and larger faith in his statesmanship. But they know that if Mr. Gladst me is defeated, and Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill come into power. Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill will pass a Home Rule Bill at least as complete and as far reaching as that which they now denounce when advocated by Mr. Gladstone. However the revolving seasons may adjust [the days, the Queen's birthday is always celebrated on a Saturday. On Saturday last there was the custo- mary round of dinner-giving, each of the heads of departments entertaining a group of guests more or less directly connected with their official duties. The birthday made some people acquainted with strange dinner companions. Mr. Gladstone, for example, entertained Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain, just as if nothing particular were happening and they were still colleagues on the Treasury Bench. In some circles this would have been an embarrassing incident, but I am told by one of the guests who watched the scene with amused interest that no one would have supposed from the manner of the host that a great gulf yawned between him and his two former friends, a gulf in which both the Ministry and the Parliament will presently disappear. He talked a good deal with Lord Hartington ; not so much with Mr. Chamberlain, but was beaming and brisk in his in- tercourse with either

groeuart etirla creditN,er very dayin this courtliness Ci asteonnea since at an-aes a early h had been deeply hurt by an incident that ha in the House of Commons. When the third reading e of the Arms Bill was called, Lord Hartington, ac- companied by Mr. Chamberlain, and evidently act- ing in concert, rose and walked down the full length of the House, refusing his assistance to the Government in passing the Bill. This is a step that might at a pinch have been excusable in Mr. Cham- berlain, he having always declarbd against any- thing in the shape of coercion. But Lord Harting- ton has always been on the side of strengthening the executive. He has now embarked upon a course which if carried unchecked to its natural end, will result in a much more stringent Arms Bill I than that just passed by the Government. That he should openly and deliberately refuse his assist-. ance to them on the present occasion could be taken only, as it was generally accepted, as an in- dication that he had broken altogether with his former colleagues and was prepared to assume to- wards them an attitude of unvaried hostility. Mr. Gladstone, it is said, was deeply hurt at this wan- ton demonstration. But no trace of the annoyance was visible, as on Saturday night he played the host to Lord Hartington's somewhat surly assump- tion of the character of guest. The great gathering of the day took place at the Foreign Office. Thither strayed all the guests from

Mrs. Broughton (of Armstrong case notoriety) died at her house in Charloss-street, Lisson-grove, on Wednesday, after suffering from dri-psy for mouths. Arricurr TO WRECK • TRAIN.—On Tuesday night a daring attempt was made to wreck the London mail train from London Road Station, MaHcbester. Obstructives had been placed on the rails close to Wimslow Station, but were detected in time to enable signals to be given for the stop- rage of the train. No motive for the crime has been found.

REMARICABLII FIND OF Conrs.—Labonrers were digging the foundation of a building in Aberdeen, on Monday, and when about three feet from the surface they discovered a bronze pet containing about 15,000 English coins ef the reign of Edward I. It is supposed that this forms part of the booty secured during one of the raids into England during the twelfth century.

div.head: FXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 5, 1886
div.p: THE FXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 5, 1886

the various dinner tables. As all were in uniform their arrival added unusual brilliancy to a scene re- markable in the quietest times. I did not see Mr. Gladstone there; but Mrs. Gladstone, in her very best dress, with quite unusual display of diamonds, came moderately early and stayed late. From eleven o'clock till midnight the crowd was enormous. It took an hour to make the journey from the foot of the staircase to the principal room. But there was no crush.ing or struggling for places. It was as well to be on the staircase as anywhere else. There was light, and warmth and music and flowers, and ever i changing company. The average number of invita- tions issued for receptions at the Foreign Office is I 2,000. On Saturday 2,400 were invited, and I fancy there were not many refusals of what is, perhaps, take it for all in all, the principal event of the Lon- don season.

The personal animosity towards Mr. Gladstone, always latent in Conservative circles, has at the present moment blazed forth with periodic inten- sity. As usual,during one of these outbursts of im- potent terror, good Conservatives comfort each other with the most ludicrous stories. I remember during the Russo-Turkish war, when Mr. Disraeli was displaying his "spirited foreign policy," an article appeared in a Turkish newspaper giving a circumstantial account of Mr. Gla4stone's parent- age, showing how his father was a pork butcher, with many details of domestic life calculated to be little a man who made such a fuss about the murder of a few thousand Bulgarians. There is a story told by Conservatives just now which shows how one touch of nature makes the ignorant Turk and the educated Englishman kin. It is cited upon the authority of a noble lord, who, being a dinner guest with Mr. Gladstone, had the opportunity of Inventing the scandal. After dinner, says the noble lord, he saw Mr. Gladstone retire into one of the recesses of the drawing-room and with excited gesticulations mutter "Power ! Power !" Mrs. Gladstone, observing him, came up, took him by the arm and quietly led him out of the room. This childish nonsense seems incredible when set forth in sober print. But the story was gravely related to me as a matter of fact by one of Lord Harting- ton's supporters in the House of Commons -who had heard it in the Conservative circles he frequents. They "would not say Mr. Gladstone is in a danger- ously excitable condition ; but this incident is.very strange." Which truly it is. The political stress has told sadly on the unfortu- nate race of artists. We are now at the end of the first week of June, the season is in full swing, the Academy is crowded, but the sales have been fewer than in any former year. The loss falls—as such losses always do—on those who can least bear it. The strong men, Millais, and Leighton, and Tadema and Hook, have got better prices than they would have got a dozen years ago, and have had no difficulty in selling the contents of their studios. But the lesser lights of the art world are threatened with extinc- tion. For the last ten days, and they Are the most important ten days at the Academy, no one could tell when a General Election might come to make trade stagnant and to dis- turb the minds of art patrons from that quiet enjoyment which preludes an offer or a bid. Oddly enough, however, Rubenstein has been a sweeping success. It, was thought Liszt, coming first, would have swept all the amateurs clean, but the Russian has conquered, and the doors have been beseiged on the days of his concerts. Time has told more upon his face than on his playing. He has grown old anthugly. He used to look like a sort of a Japanese Beethoven, picturesque and moody. Now he looks barbaric and outlandish. When he was last here, me had a sort of idea one had met him before on a teapot or on a China bowl. Now, in his black clothes and very thick boots, he looks like a kind of savage schoolmaster. His success has been one of the features of a season that opened badly and promises to end worse.
LATEST NEWS.
THE POLITICAL CRISIS. The Highland Reform League at Glasgow has passed a resolution in favour of Home Rule for Scotland, with a Parliament and Executive in the Scottish capital.

The "Daily News" says, taking all matters into account, and presuming the defeat of the Govern- ment of Ireland Bill at Monday night's sitting, it is most probable that tke dissolution may take place on Saturday, the 26th inst. It is somewhat curious that the division is fixed for the anniversary, according to the day of the week, of the defeat of the Government last year on the Budget. Mr. Childers proposals were rejected on Monday, June 8. It was stated in Dublin on Friday that it is under the consideration of the Parnellite party to cill a meeting in Dublin at an early day for the purpose of formally tendering national thanks to Mr. Glad- stone, and that the question of erecting a statute to Mr. Gladstone in Dublin will be broached at the meeting. We have been requested to publish the following correspondence :- 74, Onslow Gardens, June 4th, 18S6. Dear Mr. Gladstone,—Many belonging to the Radical sec- tion of the Liberal party feel great difficulty in arriving at the exact effect of the statements made by the overnmenr, and most especially by yourself at the Foreign Office, and suberquentiv as to the meaning of a vote in favour of the second reading of the Irish Government Bill, and the ex- tent to which it carries with it an affirmation of the specific proposals contained in the Bill relating to the mode of effec- ting and regulating autonomy in Ireland. A further differ- ence of opinion exists relative to the extent to which the Government intend to adhere to the provisions of the pre- sent bill, in framing the bill which they propose to intro- duce in an autumn session. The interpretation which I personally have given to the expressions of the Govern- ment in these matters is as follows :—First, that in voting for the second reading of the present bill, one is affirming only the principle of the establishment in Ireland of a legislative body for the conduct of Irish as distinguished from Imperial affairs; second, that the Government will consider and hold themselves free to

accept any proposals made to them prior to the introduction of the autumn bill, consistent with the five main conditions laid down by them as the essential principles of the solu- tion of the question, and their assurances as to the represen- tation of Ireland at Wt stminster on Imperial subjects. The great gravity of toe crisis and the paramount importance of a clear understanding as to the issue before the House lead me to ask you whether this interpretation correctly represents the position taken up by the Govern- ment, and must be my excuse for thus troubling you, yours most sincerely,
J. FLETCHER AIOULTON.

div.head: WIDKES ATHLETIC CLUB SPCRTS.
div.p: WIDKES ATHLETIC CLUB SPCRTS.

The lgth annual sports of ihe Widnes Athletic Club commenced last night in the show field, Farnworth, and there is every prospect that this popular fixture will be attended with the success that has characteris,d it in the past. There were upwards of 400 entrles, a number equal to previous years, although two events—the quarter-note hurdle race and the two miles flat race handicap—have been this year eliminated Wte. the programme. George, Myers, and Snooks, who have on many occasions added glory to the meeting, are now nct able to appear under the 'rules of the N C.A.A., having joined the ranks of the professionals. There are, however, several champions on the track to ap- pear to-day, and the events will be fraught with exciting interest. J. M. Cowie, the 100 yards champion, will ap- pear, and other sprinters are A. Wharton, a mullatto, of Darlington, awl Bishop, of Netts Forest. In the long dis- tance contests 1). S. Last night was reserved for purely diatrict competitions;, but notwith- standing the merely local interest attachinz ro the cont,ste, over two thousand persons paid for admission to the ground, the weather fortunately being fine, although cold. The arrangements show the usual completeness, whilst the officers are men of experience and judgment. The im- portant duty of handicapper and rezeree was filled by Mr. Walter Platt, and Mr. T. div.head: CHESHIRE GENTLEMAN KILLED
div.p: A CHESHIRE GENTLEMAN KILLED
ON TIIE RAILWAY.

On Thursday afternoon, as the 4-35 train from Huddersfield to Manchester was leaving Hudders- field station, a gentleman, apparently about 45 years of age, was cbserved to run forward and try to get into one of the carriages. In this he was unsuccessful, and he fell between the footboard of the carriage and the platform, and was dragged for a considerable distance before the train was stopped. He was smashed almost to pieces, and was quite dead when picked up, A handkerchief found on him bore the name of "S. Rowlands," and he had in his pocket the return half of a ticket from Warrington to llarrogate. On Thunday night, Mr. Ashurst, stationmaster at Bank Quay, received information of the accident, and particulars given led to the belief that the de- ceased lived somewhere about Warrington. It was ascertained from one of the porters that a Mr. Row- lands, who lived somewhere in Cheshire, had with ; his wife entered a train at Bank Quay Station on I the 24th May. A porter was despatched to Dares- bury, and from the stationmaster it was learned that a gentleman named Rowlands lived at Dares- bury, and it was also discovered that his son, with his wife, had gone to Harrogate for a short time. From this it is thought that deceased is Mr. S. Rowlands, a gentleman of large means, who resided at Grimsditch Hall, near Whitley, Cheshire. It is stated that he was a shareholder to the extent of £15,000 in the London and North-Western Railway. No doubt appears to be entertained in this neigh- bourhood as to the identity of the deceased, and it is stated that Mrs. Rowlands has gone to Hud- dersfield lo identify the body of the unfortunate gentleman.

A DISTURBANCE AT MUCR WOOLTON.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Captain Willis and Mr. H. James Gallagher. of Much Woolton, was charged ua; Brig der it h' warrant with a breach of the peace on the 31et October ; he was further Charged with drunkenness on Mon- day, and also with asqattiting P.C.'s Samuel Blackburn and John Timperley. The constables were apprebending the prisoner on Monday under a warrant for breach of tbe peace, when he become very violent and kicked both officers.— Superintendent Barker said the prisoner was a terror to the neighbourhood, and read along liqt of previous convictions Against him.— The Bench imposed a fine of lOs and costs or 14 days' imprisonment; and in one case of assault inflicted a fine of 20s and costs, or one month's imprisonment. The other cases were dismissed.

Archdeacon stack, Rector of Monaghan has been elected Bishop of Clongher. The Duke of Cambridge reviewed the troops at Alder- shot, on Frilay, in favourable weather. seven thousand troops paraded. At Killarmy, on Thursday night, a caretaker named Ric- kard Tangy was shot in the legs by two moonlighters, dying in a few hours afterwards. At Lords, on Friday. the gentlemen's second innings ter- minated for 136 runs. The Australians went in. and haying made 86 mere, they consequently won by seven wickets. ALLEGED DYNAMITE OUTRAGES.—A Paris correspondent says : A telegram from Decazeville states that several more attempts have been made to blow up with dynamite the houses of miners who have returned to work against the wishes of the strikers. No one has yet been killed, but there has been considerable destruction to property. The landlords have resolved to keep watch during the night. TERRIBLE MACHINERY ACCIDENT.—A dreadful accident occurred on Friday morning at the Patent Fuel Works of Messrs. Cory, Yeo, and Co., Swansea. A pitch* grinder, named Richard Ladd, by some means or other was drawn under the rollers of a machine, and before he could be extricated it was found necessary to amputate one of his legs. The poor fellow died a few minutes after his release.

THE MISSING AMERICAN GENTLEMAN.—A despatch has been received at New York by the friends of 111 r. Nouree, who se mysteriously disappeared in England, stating that he is alive. It is explained that Mr. Nourse left the train at a station between London and Liverpool, and carefully concealed his whereabouts, in order to make his friends be- lieve he was dead. His object in doing so is unknown. His friends are reticent, but they believe the story. THE GBEAT MAIL BAG ROBBERY.—At the Old Bailey, on Friday, A charge against Henry Andrews of being in possession of three Russian one hundred rouble notes, part of the property stolen from the continental mail on April 8, was fuither proceeded with. The evidence given on the previous day was almost entirely that of witnesses who de- posed to the mail bags being duly delivered at Ostend from the steamer Marie Louise to the railway train, and showing they were not tampered with there. The cross-examination on Friday elicited no new facts.
SHOCRING AFFRAY BETWEEN ORANGEMEN AND CATHOLICS.

In an affray between Orangemen and -Catholics at the Queen's Island shipbuilding yard, Be:fast, on Friday after- noon, a dozen of the latter were wounded, and several are reported missing, having been thrown into the water. In- tense excitement prevails. Another correspondent says : A serious attack was made upon a gang of fifty Catholic workmen employed in the excavation of a new graving dock by a great body of Queen Ireland Protestant workingmen, estimated by a police offi- cial at 2 000 strong. A dozen men were injured, four of them badly, and one or two lads are said to have been drowned. The Catholic workmen are leaving work fearing a revival of mischief. The attack arose out of a quarrel be. tween a Catholic and Protestant workman at Harland and Wolfs shipbuilding yard on Thursday afternoon. A row followed, and in consequence of the disturbance both parties to the quarrel were aischarged. On Friday afternoon a great body of lads and men employed in the shipbuilding yards who had occupied only a quarter of an hour over their dinner suddenly appeared at the graving dock works armed with sticks, iron rods. shovels, and stones, and raising cries against the Papists/ushed upon the surprised Catholic workmen and wounded 4 number of them. One man being called upon to curse the Pope, and declaring that he would not curse anybody, was badly beaten about the head, and other men were thrown down and had stones cast at them. On my way to the scenes I met several cars conveying men with bloodstained faces to the hospitals. Some men were said to have been chased into the water, and one man was crying for the loss of his young brother. The wives of the Catholic workmen having heard of the disturbance came to meet them, and they complained that the Protestant workmen had insulted them on theic way. The originators of .the attack were rivetters' boys, who drew out the men. The police authorities of Armagh have forwarded to Dub- lin Castle full particulars of the drilling of Orangemen at Richball, near Armagh, together with the n-mes of those taking part therein.

CONSTANTINOPLE, FRIDAY.—The Porte has issued a cir- cular to the Powers declaring its satsfaction at the Greek disarmament, and requesting the Powers to raise the blockade.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Royal assent was givn by Com- mission to 44 public and private bills, including the Peace Preservation (Ireland) Continuance Act.—The Marquis of SALISBURY complained that the Irish Secretary last night and Mr. Blaine misquoted him with regard to a coercive policy towards Ireland. and assisting Irish to emigrate. He did not mind abase, but desired to be quoted accurately. —Earl KIMBERLEY thought the language capable of the construction put on it by Mr. Morley.—The subject then dropped, and the House adjourned. HOUSE Or COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. THE GOLD COAST.—Mr. OSBORNE MORGAN, replying to Mr. Hutton. said he was not aware that trade on the Gold Coast was in a ruinous condition. No disturbance had taken place between the natives or the British and the natives. • COLONIAL FEDERATION.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Mr. Howard Vincent, thought the present time was auspi- cious for nolding a conference upon Colenial Federation, more especially as there was not a single colonial Prime Minister armed with the necessary powers now in this country.—Mr. BADEN POWELL asked whether, in view of the loyal share taken by the colonies in the defence of the empire, the Government would arrange for a naval review on a large scale in order that many distinguished colonists now in this country might have the opportunity of witness- ing a muster of ironclads and other vessels representative of the naval strength of the empire.—Mr. GLADSTONE said if such review was to be held it ought to be done on a large scale, and that at the present moment would be inconve- nient to the public service. He thought it would be well for our distinguished visitors to inspect the naval construc- tion departments of the Royal navy, and every facility would be given to those who chose to do so. THE HOME RULE BILL. The adjourned debate on the motion for the second read- ing of the Government of Ireland Bill was resumed. Mr. ILLINGWORTH supported the second reading of the bill, and deprecated the action of those of the Liberal patty favourable to the principle of the measure voting against the second reading. The Prime Minister had been some- what toe hasty in promising to remodel the 24th clause. Having done so, he thought he was entitled to some confi- dence in return. He could see nothing in the bill to en- danger the supremacy of Parliament or the integrity of the empire, although he did not think they could at present boast much of the unity that existed. He favoured the change proposed in the bill, and if passed, he looked confi- dently for the most favourable results. Mr. H. TROTTER thought the House must feel that they were not asked to essist in passing a law but in saving a Government. He did not believe that the bill would really be accepted AS a final settlement, and there was no ground for the insinuation that if the Conservatives came into power they would be prepared to pass a measure to the slightest degree approaching the bill under discussion ; and be ventured to say if the leaders were to bring in that mo- tion they would not be supported by the rank and file of the party. He thought that measure was bad in iteelf, opposed to the spirit of the times, that it WAS an attempt to put back the band of the clock. Mr. OSBORNE MortGAN defended the proposals of the bill and insisted that its proposals were wise and just. He said it was childish to deny that the Irish people were over- whelming in favour of Home Rule. During the five months that the Conservatives were in power Ireland was not gov- erned at all. The law, as they themselves acknowledged, bad fallen into contempt, and it was absolutely impossible that such a state of things could be allowed to continue. It was, he insisted, impossible to govern Ireland as Lord Salisbury proposed. All that members would be voting for In assenting to the second reading would be.tbe transfer to Dublin of Irish business which bad been a bane and curse to the Imperial Parliament. • Colonel KING HARMAN opposed the bill, the effect of which, if passed, would be to drain capital from Ireland, and a great increase of taxatioß in England. Ihe Bill, say what they might, was a measure of separation. Mr. NEwietts gave his hearty support to the second read- ing.—Mr. EVELYN WHITE, opposing the bill, thought the division might have been very well taken at that sitting. [Lister sirrnen.l

• THE FIRST CONCEAT of Mr. Oreste James Praeger, junr., is advertised to take place at the Co-opera- tive Hall next Tuesday evening. THE REV. JOHN YONGE has returned from Llan- dudno, where he has been staying for several weeks in consequelitce of ill-health. He has made consi- derable improvement, but, we regret to say, he is still far from well.

THE POOR Box.—At the Borough Police Cuurt, on Wednesday, on the application of Chief Constable Hunt, the magistrates directed that a shilling that had come into the possession of the police under somewhat unusual circumstances should be put in. the poor box at the Police Court. A prisoner was being conveyed to gaol from Warrington when a person in the street handed him a shilling with which to purchase liquor before going into prison. The constable took charge of the shilling, and, it being illegal for anything to be handed to a pri- soner while being conveyed to gaol, the Bench or- dered it to be disposed of as stated. SUSPECTED THIEVES.—Michael Callighan, . a young man who has given the police some trouble, was brought before the borough magistrates on Monday, charged as a reputed thief, with being found loitering in Bank-street early on Sunday morning, with intent to commit a felony. Inspector Berry said that prisoner Was one of a class of men who set upon innocent men in the streets after dark and stole what they could. The Bench sent Calli- ghan to prison for two months.—Martin Cross, charged at the same court, with being on the en- closed premises of Mr. R. A. Naylor, Howley, Quay, on the previous morning, with intent to commit a felony, was sent to prison for 14 days.

THE QUEEN'S BIETHDAX.—On Saturday after- noon the local volunteers celebrated the Queen's 67th birthday by firing a feu de foie in the drill field. near Walton Arches. The men mustered in good force at the Drill Hall at 4-30, and marched thence to the field, where they went through several manceuvres in a manner that was very creditable and gave testimony to their efficiency as a corps. The progress of the volunteers through the town both going to, and returning from, the field, was watched by a considerable number of people, and the men, as they'marched past, looked very smart and soldierly. The following were the ofilcers pre- sent :—Major and Adjutant O'Leary (in command), Captains' Ridgway, Widdows, Thomson, and Gooch ;Lieutenant Baynes, Quartermaster Hutchin- son, and Surgeon Gornall.

MR. GEORGE SANGER'S vIRCIITS.--04 Monday afternoon there was a large turn-out of spectators, young and old, to witness the procession in connec- with the circus of Mr. G. Sangers, which visited Warrington that day,. The procession did not belie the reputation of this renowned circus, as it was a very long one and comprised a herd of huge elephants and a number of uncouth camels, gigantic triumphal cars drawn by long yokes of draught horses, and smaller vehicles to which were attached strings of diminutive ponies. In addition there was an imposing display of male and female performers in equestrian habits riding on well-conditioned ani- mals, and a number of shapely performing. horses, led by grooms.. The display was much admired. The circus tent was erected in the Post-office field, off Sankey-street, and here well-attended first-class performances were given in the afternoon and evening.

HAYNES'S, FOR YOUR WALKING DAY SHOES. CAIRO-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The anniver- sary of this school was celebrated on Sunday. In connection with the event sermons were preached morning and evening in the chapel by the Rev. J. Estlin Carpenter, M.A., of Manchester New College, London, and in the afternoon a suitable address was made to the children by the Rev. R. Pilcher, B.A. The chapel presented a very beautiful appearance, having been profusely embellished with flowers by the ladies of the sewhig class. Bunches of flowers were placed at the end of each pew, in the win- dows, and in front of the pulpit. The front of the pulpit in particular had been very tastefully .adorned, some of the flowers used for the purpose of embellishment being rare and handsome. Each of the services was well attended, although that of the afternoon .was not favoured with propitious weather. Special hymns were sung at each ser- vice. The collections of the day amounted to £lB ss.

ALLEGED IMPUDENT THEFT BY A CARD SHAR- PER.—At the Borough Court, on Tuesday, Joseph Corcoran, Bank-street, described by Chief Constable Hunt as a card sharper and thimble rigger, was com- mitted for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on a charge of stealing a purse containing half a sov- ereign and a florin, from the person of William Johnson, farm labourer, Sutton Weaver, Cheshire, on the 31st of last month. Prosecutor, according to the evidence, came to Warrington in company with another farm labourer named Martin Caulfield, of Newton-by-Daresbury, and at about nine o'clock in the evening the two went to the Gun Inn, Scotland- road, where they saw the prisoner. Prosecutor had a purse in his pocket containing half a sovereign and a florin, and prisoner seized hold of him and took it out of his pocket. He handed prosecutor the purse back, but the money was nct in it. In- formation was given to the police and prisoner was arrested.

"IRISHMEN TO THE FRONT."-At the Borough Court. on Monday, a young man named James Con- cannon, was brought up in custody on charges of being drunk and disorderly in Bewsey-street on Saturday night, and of assaulting P.S. Bowen and John Duckworth. The police-sergeant said that he was on Saturday night walking in Bewsey-street, in the direction of liorsemarket-street, when he saw a large crowd assembled. Prisoner was there in a drunken condition, and some men were trying to persuade him to go home. Witness also told him to do so, but prisoner refused and struck him on the mouth. The sergeant procured assistance from the crowd, and prisoner was taken to the Police Station. On the way he shouted "Now, Irishmen, to the front. Is there no one here will put a bit of lead through him to release me? Where's young Ireland?" When at the cells, prisoner kicked tho sergeant on the cap of the knee. It was also stated that he assaulted Duckworth.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s and costs.

Tetal 3B Total 142 WARRINGTON v. NEWTON IND GROUND.—This match was played on Saturday on the Arpley Ground. A severe storm compelled the players to wait unit! after four o'clock, whee a start was made. J. C. Lawton and J. J. Crosfield commenced the Warrington innings against Hindley and the Newton professional. Lawton was soon run out, and Clarke joined Crosfield, who was playing very steadily. At 66 t.larke was (taught at point, and a long stand was made by C. G. Lawton and Crosfield. Both played steady cricket, but hit freely when necessary. The latter played just over two hours, scoring 43, and he well deserved the congra- tulations awarded him. His innings was without a mistake, and marked by oa,tient defensive play. Lawton was joined by Knowles and Ford, but at drawing of stumps was still not oat at 82. His hitting all round was clean, hard, and true ; and approached nearly his form of last year, when he was so successful. WARRINGTON. The Lancashire and Derbyshire elevens were unfortunate as regards weather in their match at Old Trafford, which had to be abandoned on Saturday afternoon, play having been eltegether prevented on Thursday and much inter- fered with on Friday. On the second day each county had completed one innings, Derbyshire for 4-0 and Lancashire for 97, while the former had lost one wicket in their second attempt for 19. When the game was stopped two other wickets had fallen, and the total was only up to 27. The match between Yorkshire and Sussex ended at Hud- dersfield on Saturday in a draw in favour of Yorkshire, Sussex having at the finish six wickets to fall and wanting 199 runs to win. Overnight Sussex, going in against a total of 93, had lost three wickets for eight runs, and on Saturday morning the other 'batsmen were all dismissed for a total of 46. The second innings of Yorkshire produced some interesting cricket. Hall went in first and was not out at the finish, his innings of 50 lasting four hours. He hit a five to leg, three fours, four threes, and six twos. Bates, who went in first wicket down at two, scored 63 out of the next 89 runs. His figures were six fours, two threes, and twelve twos. After the fall of the eighth wicket, at 134, Peate hit up 30 in very vigorous style. Rain fell so heavily after the close of the innings that it seemed likely there would be no more play. The weather improved, how- ever, and Sussex went in for 40 minutes' batting. Before the bowling of Peate and Emmett the southern county fared very badly, and lost four wickets for 22 runs before the match was left drawn. The ground at Old Trafford, where North of England met Australia, was swamped on Tuesday, and on Wednes- day it was found to be in such a condition as to render play out of the question; and early in the afternoon the match was abandoned. After a well-fought game Middlesex beat Kent at Lord's, on Wednesday, by 43 runs. Overnight Kent, with all ten wickets to fall in their second innings, had been left with 133 to get to win. This task proved rather beyond the abilities of the team, who took three hours and ten minutes to score 89 runs. Although Notts only wanted 51 runs to win against Sus- sex and had all their wickets in hand, at Brighton, on Wednesday, it took an hour and thirty-five minnee and they lost three wickets in obtaining them. The gussex bowlers were all seen to advantage. Bean, who is likely to preve very valuable to Sussex, took eight wickets for 63 runs. In the result Notts won by seven wickets. The Parsees may be having a very nice holiday in Eng- land, and no doubt they are enjoying the delights of Wes- tern civilisation, but as cricketers they are about equal to a second eleven of a village school. There are one or two of them who have learned to bat in pretty good style, and most of them field fairly well when the ball does not come to them. With the exception of Mr. Framjee, who bowls in fairly good form, and Mr. Major, who keeps the ball a good length and is at times rather difficult when the ground helps him, they can do nothing at cricket. In fielding these wealthy gentlemen from Bombay generally look at the ball, and if nobody else betrays in any wise an anxiety to run after it the man who happens to be nearest to it generally trots in that direction. They have a few fixed ideas, and they do the wrong thing with a persistent regularity that would be gratifying to the spectators if It were not quite so comic. Still, they have not come to show us cricket— which is fortunate for us—and if they really mean to try and learn they have that great advantage which all learners should possess—an abundant supply of ignorance to dispel. , —"Manchester Guardian.”
